Conditions to Closing General Conditions Consummation of the Transactions is conditioned on the approval of the condition precedent proposals (as defined above) by CCXI shareholders described in this proxy statement/prospectus, and the adoption and approval of the Merger Agreement and the approval of the Merger and the other Transactions by the requisite consent of Agility’s stockholders. In addition, the consummation of the Transactions contemplated by the Merger Agreement is conditioned upon, among other things: • the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the HSR Act; • no governmental authority having jurisdiction over any party or the Transactions will have issued any order, judgment, injunction, decree, writ, stipulation, determination or award, in each case, entered by or with any governmental authority preventing, materially restraining, enjoining or otherwise prohibiting the consummation of the transactions contemplated by the Merger Agreement, and no law will have been enforced that prevents or materially restrains the consummation of the Transactions; • the adoption or execution and delivery of any organizational documents or agreements necessary to give effect to the governance arrangements contemplated by the Merger Agreement and Transaction Agreements; • the taking of all action such that the Post -Closing Company Board as of immediately following the Closing will be comprised of the directors contemplated by the Merger Agreement; • the shares of Post -Closing Company common stock having been listed on Nasdaq and being eligible for continued listing on Nasdaq immediately following the Closing; and 5 Table of Contents • this registration statement having become effective in accordance with the Securities Act, no stop order having been issued by the SEC with respect to the registration statement and no action seeking such order having been threatened or initiated. CCXI’s Conditions to Closing The obligations of CCXI and Merger Sub to consummate the Transactions contemplated by the Merger Agreement also are conditioned upon, among other things: • the accuracy of the representations and warranties of Agility as of the Closing, subject to applicable materiality standards set forth in the Merger Agreement; • the covenants of Agility in the Merger Agreement required to be performed as of or prior to the Closing having been performed in all material respects; • since the date of the Merger Agreement, there must not have occurred a Material Adverse Effect (as defined in the Merger Agreement) with respect to Agility which is continuing; and • the last day of the 20 -day period during which appraisal must be demanded as contemplated by Section 262(d)(2) of the DGCL (the “ Appraisal Rights Deadline ”) will have occurred and no holders of Agility capital stock, individually or in the aggregate, beneficially owning more than five percent of the issued and outstanding shares of Agility capital stock (with such number of shares being calculated, with respect to the Agility preferred stock, on an as -converted to Agility common stock basis) will beneficially own any Dissenting Shares as of the Closing. Agility’s Conditions to Closing The obligations of Agility to consummate the Transactions also are conditioned upon, among other things: • the accuracy of the representations and warranties of CCXI and Merger Sub as of the Closing, subject to applicable materiality standards set forth in the Merger Agreement; • the covenants of CCXI and Merger Sub in the Merger Agreement required to be performed as of or prior to the Closing having been performed in all material respects; • the Minimum Cash Condition having been met; • the Domestication having been completed as provided in the Merger Agreement and a time -stamped copy of the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation issued by the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware in relation thereto having been delivered to Agility; • since the date of the Merger Agreement, there must not have occurred a SPAC Material Adverse Effect with respect to CCXI which is continuing; and • the covenants of the Sponsor and the Insiders under the Sponsor Agreement having been performed in all material respects, and no such Sponsor or Insider having threatened (orally or in writing) (1) that the Sponsor Agreement is not valid, binding and in full force and effect, (2) that CCXI or Agility is in breach of or default under the Sponsor Agreement or (3) to terminate the Sponsor Agreement. Waiver Any party to the Merger Agreement may, at any time prior to the Closing, by action taken by its board of directors or equivalent governing body, or officers thereunto duly authorized, waive in writing any of its rights or conditions in its favor under the Merger Agreement. The existence of the financial and personal interests of the directors may result in a conflict of interest on the part of one or more of them between what such director may believe is best for CCXI and what such director may believe is best for such director in determining whether or not to grant a waiver in a specific situation. 6 Table of Contents Termination The Merger Agreement may be terminated and the Transactions abandoned prior to the Closing, as follows: • by mutual written consent of CCXI and Agility; • by CCXI if the Transactions are not consummated on or before December 31, 2026 (the “ Termination Date ”), which date may be automatically extended in the event that any action or legal proceeding for specific performance or other equitable relief by any party with respect to the Merger Agreement, any other Transaction Agreement, or otherwise with respect to the Transactions is commenced or pending on or before December 31, 2026, in which case the Termination Date will be extended until the date that is 30 days following the date on which a final, non -appealable order or judgment has been entered with respect to such action or legal proceeding, provided that CCXI’s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended); • by Agility if the Transactions are not consummated on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended), provided that Agility’s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended); and provided, further, that, Agility will use reasonable best efforts to provide written notice to CCXI, in good faith, prior to the Domestication, if Agility believes it has the right to, and intends to, terminate the Merger Agreement prior to the closing of the Transactions; • by either CCXI or Agility if the other party has breached any of its covenants, agreements, representations or warranties which would cause the conditions to the Closing not to be satisfied and has not cured its breach, if curable, within 30 days of receiving written notice of such breach, provided that the terminating party’s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before such date; • by either CCXI or Agility if a final, non -appealable governmental order or a statute, rule or regulation permanently enjoins or prohibits consummation of the Merger; • by either CCXI or Agility if the approval by CCXI shareholders of the proposals voted on at the extraordinary general meeting and required to consummate the Transactions is not obtained at the extraordinary general meeting (subject to any adjournment or postponement thereof), provided that CCXI is not entitled to terminate on these grounds if, at the time of such termination, CCXI is in breach of its obligations under the Merger Agreement with respect to this proxy statement/prospectus and the stockholders’ meeting; • by CCXI in the event the Agility stockholders holding Agility capital stock sufficient to obtain the Company Stockholder Approval (as defined in the Merger Agreement) fail to deliver the Agility stockholder written consent within 48 hours of the registration statement becoming effective, provided that this right to terminate the Merger Agreement will not be available if the Company Stockholder Approval is obtained prior to CCXI providing notice of its intent to terminate the Merger Agreement on account of a Written Consent Failure (as defined in the Merger Agreement); or • by Agility if the CCXI Board changes, withdraws, withholds, qualifies or modifies (or publicly proposes to do so) its recommendation to CCXI shareholders to approve certain matters related to the Transactions. Effect of Termination In the event of proper termination by either CCXI or Agility, the Merger Agreement will become void and have no effect (other than with respect to certain surviving provisions specified in the Merger Agreement), without any liability under the Merger Agreement on the part of any party thereto or its respective affiliates, officers, directors, employees, representatives or stockholders, other than liability of any party thereto for any intentional and willful breach of the Merger Agreement by such party occurring prior to such termination. 7 Table of Contents Fees and Expenses All fees and expenses incurred in connection with the Merger Agreement and the Transactions, except for those fees associated with the filing to obtain clearance pursuant to the HSR Act, will be paid by the party incurring such expenses whether or not the Transactions will be consummated; except that if the Closing occurs, CCXI will bear and pay at or promptly after the Closing: • all CCXI transaction expenses; and • all Agility transaction expenses; provided that all costs of investigation and all defense and attorneys’ and other professional fees and settlement payments related to stockholder actions initiated by or on behalf of any stockholders of Agility, whether borne by CCXI or Agility, will be fully payable by the Post -Closing Company if the closing of the Transactions occurs and not subject to any limitation or cap. All fees and expenses in connection with filing to obtain clearance pursuant to the HSR Act will be paid by CCXI. Incentive Plan and ESPP Incentive Plan The CCXI Board will approve the Incentive Plan, subject to the approval of the CCXI shareholders. The Incentive Plan will initially reserve for issuance a number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock equal to 13% of the fully diluted, and as converted, outstanding Post -Closing Company common stock immediately following the consummation of the business combination, subject to certain adjustments and an evergreen provision. The purpose of the Incentive Plan is to provide a means whereby the Post -Closing Company can secure and retain the services of employees, directors and consultants; to provide incentives for such persons to exert maximum efforts for the success of the Post -Closing Company and its affiliates and to provide a means by which such persons may be given an opportunity to benefit from increases in value of the Post -Closing Company common stock through the granting of awards under the Incentive Plan. A copy of the Incentive Plan is included as Annex E to this proxy statement/prospectus. See the section entitled “ Proposal No. 6 — The Incentive Plan Proposal .” ESPP The CCXI Board will approve the ESPP, subject to the approval of the CCXI shareholders. The ESPP will initially reserve for issuance a number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock equal to 2% of the fully diluted, and as converted outstanding Post -Closing Company common stock immediately following the consummation of the business combination, subject to certain adjustments and an evergreen provision. The purpose of the ESPP is to provide a means whereby the Post -Closing Company can align the long -term financial interests of its employees with the financial interests of its stockholders. A copy of the ESPP is included as Annex F to this proxy statement/prospectus. A quorum for such meeting will consist of the holders present by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy of shares of CCXI representing at least one -third (1/3) of the paid up voting share capital of CCXI entitled to vote at such meeting. Proxies that are marked “abstain” will be treated as shares of CCXI public shares present for purposes of determining the presence of a quorum on all matters. Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. The Sponsor owns of record and is entitled to vote % of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares ( % of the outstanding CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares and % of the outstanding CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date. Such shares, as well as any shares of CCXI public shares acquired in the aftermarket by the Sponsor, will be voted in favor of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. The proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting will require the following votes: • the approval of each of the business combination proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and, if presented, the adjournment proposal require approval by ordinary resolution, being the affirmative vote of a simple majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder’s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the business combination proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and, if presented, the adjournment proposal will have no effect on such proposals; • the approval of the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal require approval by special resolution, being the affirmative vote of holders of at least two -thirds of the CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder’s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal will have no effect on such proposals. Under the CCXI current articles of association, CCXI’s directors have the authority to resolve that CCXI be registered by way of continuation in a jurisdiction outside the Cayman Islands or such other jurisdiction in which it is for the time being incorporated, registered or existing (including, but not limited to, the approval of the organizational documents to be adopted by the Company in such other jurisdiction to the extent applicable). Accordingly, it is not necessary for CCXI to receive shareholder consent to the Domestication, and the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal are therefore being presented to CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only; and • with respect to the director election proposal, directors are elected by a majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote thereon at the extraordinary general meeting. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder’s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting or a withhold vote with regard to a director nominee named in the director election proposal will have no effect on such proposal. The business combination proposal, the domestication proposal, the organizational documents proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and the director election proposal are referred to as the “ condition precedent proposals .” Each condition precedent proposal is conditioned on the approval of each of the condition precedent proposals. Therefore, if any of the condition precedent proposals are not approved at the extraordinary general meeting (or any adjournment or postponement thereof), none of the other condition precedent proposals will have any effect, even if approved by the requisite holders of CCXI Ordinary Shares. It is important for you to note that in the event that any of those proposals are not approved, then unless certain conditions in the Merger Agreement are waived by the applicable parties to the Merger Agreement, the Merger Agreement may be terminated and the business combination may not be consummated. 13 Table of Contents Redemption Rights Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, a holder of CCXI public shares may demand that CCXI redeem such shares for cash if the business combination is consummated. Such redemption rights are not available to the Sponsor, officers or directors. Eligible holders of CCXI public shares will be entitled to receive cash for these shares only if they demand in writing that CCXI redeem their CCXI public shares for cash no later than the Redemption Deadline by delivering their shares and requesting in writing that CCXI redeem such CCXI public shares for cash to Continental Stock Transfer & Trust Company, CCXI’s transfer agent. If the business combination is not completed, the CCXI public shares will not be redeemed. If an eligible holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises their redemption rights and the business combination is consummated, CCXI will redeem such shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds in the trust account, calculated as of two business days prior to the consummation of the business combination and net of certain permitted withdrawals. As of the CCXI record date, this would amount to approximately $ per share. In such case, such holder of CCXI public shares will be exchanging their shares for cash and will no longer own such shares. Please see the section entitled “ Extraordinary General Meeting of CCXI — Redemption Rights ” for a detailed description of the procedures to be followed if you wish to redeem your CCXI public shares for cash. Notwithstanding the foregoing, a holder of CCXI public shares, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a “group” (as defined in Section 13(d)(3) of the Exchange Act), will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the CCXI public shares. Accordingly, all CCXI public shares in excess of 15% held by a CCXI public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a “group,” will not be redeemed without the prior consent of our directors. Pursuant to the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have agreed to waive their redemption rights with respect to all of their CCXI Ordinary Shares in connection with the consummation of the business combination and, because of this, such CCXI Ordinary Shares are excluded from the pro rata calculation used to determine the per share redemption price. As is customary in transactions of this type, the Sponsor and the Insiders did not receive any consideration for waiving their redemption rights. The Transactions are subject to these requirements and may not be completed until the expiration of a 18 Table of Contents 30 -day waiting period following the filing of the required Notification and Report Forms with the Antitrust Division and the FTC or until early termination is granted. If the FTC or the Antitrust Division issues a Request for Additional Information or Documentary Material (a “ Second Request ”) within the initial 30 -day waiting period, the waiting period with respect to the Transactions will be extended for an additional period of 30 calendar days, which will begin on the date on which the filing parties each certify compliance with the Second Request. There is no assurance that the Antitrust Division, the FTC, any state attorney general, or any other government authority will not attempt to challenge the Transactions on antitrust grounds, and, if such a challenge is made, we cannot assure you as to its result. Summary Risk Factors Agility’s business is subject to a number of risks of which you should be aware before making a decision to invest in our securities. These risks include, among others, the following: • Agility’s business plans require a significant amount of capital. Agility’s future capital needs may require Agility to sell additional equity or debt securities that may dilute its stockholders or introduce covenants that may restrict its operations or its ability to pay dividends. • Agility has very limited experience commercializing its products and may not be able to do so efficiently or effectively. • Agility relies on a limited number of customers for a significant portion of potential revenue, and the loss of any one of these customers may adversely affect Agility’s business, financial condition and results of operations. • Agility operates in a competitive industry that is subject to rapid technological change, and Agility expects competition to increase. • It is possible that the unit economics of Agility’s humanoid robot solutions do not materialize as expected, which could significantly hinder Agility’s ability to generate a commercially viable product at scale and adversely affect Agility’s business prospects. See the section entitled “ Unaudited Prospective Unit Economics Information ” for more information. • Agility relies on global supply chains and disruptions could delay production, increase costs, and limit Agility’s ability to fulfill customer orders. Changes in trade policy, including tariffs and “Buy American” requirements, could further disrupt Agility’s supply chain and raise input costs. • Design flaws, defects, software errors, or unintended AI -driven behaviors could result in product recalls, injury to co -located workers, product liability claims, and significant litigation expenses. • The regulatory framework for robotics, AI -enabled products, and humanoid robots operating in shared workspaces is rapidly evolving. Failure to comply with new or changing regulations — including evolving AI -governance laws, industrial safety standards, and privacy requirements — could lead to product withdrawal, increased costs, or restrictions on deployment. 19 Table of Contents • Agility’s success depends in part on its ability to obtain and maintain protection for the intellectual property relating to or incorporated into its products. Agility may be subject to intellectual property infringement claims or misappropriation claims, which may be time -consuming and expensive and, if adversely determined, could limit Agility’s ability to commercialize its products. • Agility is subject to cybersecurity risks to operational systems, security systems, infrastructure, integrated software and partners’ and customers’ data processed by Agility or third -party vendors or suppliers and any material failure, weakness, interruption, cyber event, incident or breach of security may prevent Agility from effectively operating its business. Further, issues relating to Agility’s use of AI, combined with an uncertain legal and regulatory environment, may adversely affect Agility’s business, financial condition and results of operations. • The issuance of shares of the Post -Closing Company’s securities in connection with private placement will dilute the voting power of the Post -Closing Company’s shareholders. • Churchill and Agility will incur significant transaction costs in connection with the business combination, and the incurrence of these costs will reduce the amount of cash available to be used for other corporate purposes by Churchill if the business combination is not completed. • The consummation of the business combination is subject to several conditions and if those conditions are not satisfied or waived, the business combination may not be completed. • Agility is highly dependent on the services of its senior management and other key employees and, if Agility is unable to attract and retain a sufficient number of qualified employees, its ability to design, manufacture and launch its products, operate its business and compete could be harmed. • If a significant number of Churchill’s Ordinary Shares are elected to be redeemed in connection with the business combination, the stock ownership of the Post -Closing Company will be highly concentrated, which will reduce the public “float” and may have a negative effect on the market price of the common stock of the Post -Closing Company. • Churchill’s shareholders will experience dilution as a consequence of the issuance of the Post -Closing Company’s common stock as consideration in the business combination. • The benefits of the business combination may not be realized to the extent currently anticipated by Agility and Churchill, or at all. If the business combination’s benefits do not meet the expectations of investors or securities analysts, the market price of Churchill’s securities or, following the consummation of the business combination, the value of the Post -Closing Company’s securities may decline. • After the closing of the business combination, sales of a substantial number of shares of the Post -Closing Company’s stock in the public market by existing shareholders could cause the stock price to decline. Further, after the closing of the business combination, a significant number of shares of the Post -Closing Company’s stock will be subject to issuance upon exercise of outstanding warrants, which may result in dilution to the Post -Closing Company’s shareholders. • There is no assurance that the Post -Closing Company’s securities will be approved for listing on Nasdaq or that the Post -Closing Company will be able to comply with the continued listing standards of Nasdaq. • Some of Churchill’s officers and directors and its Sponsor may have conflicts of interest that may influence or have influenced them to support or approve the business combination. • Legal proceedings in connection with the business combination, the outcomes of which are uncertain, could delay or prevent the completion of the business combination. • Changes in laws or regulations, or a failure to comply with any laws and regulations, may adversely affect Agility and the Post -Closing Company’s business and ability to consummate the business combination. Risks Related to Agility Unless the context otherwise requires, references in this subsection to “Agility,” “the Company,” “we,” “us” or “our” refer to the business of Agility and its subsidiaries prior to the consummation of the business combination, which will be the business of the Post -Closing Company and its subsidiaries following the business combination. Risks Related to Our Industry Humanoid robots are an emerging category of robotics, and customer adoption of Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and similar humanoid systems may be slower than anticipated relative to fixed industrial robots, autonomous mobile robots (“AMRs”) or other warehouse automation solutions that have longer track records and more established customer acceptance. If potential customers choose proven conventional automation over humanoid robots, Agility’s revenue growth and market penetration could be materially adversely affected. Humanoid robots represent an entirely new category of robotic systems that have not yet achieved broad commercial deployment or widespread customer acceptance. Unlike fixed industrial robots and AMRs, which have decades of proven track records in manufacturing and warehouse environments, humanoid bipedal robots such as Digit are unproven at scale and customers may be reluctant to adopt them over established automation solutions. Potential customers may perceive humanoid robots as unproven technology, lack confidence in Agility’s business model, or prefer the demonstrated reliability and lower perceived risk of conventional automation. The market for our products may not develop as expected, or may develop more slowly than anticipated, due to customer hesitancy, long evaluation cycles, or a preference for incremental automation solutions with which their workforces and operations teams are already familiar. If potential customers choose conventional automation — including AMRs, collaborative robots, or fixed material -handling equipment — over humanoid robots, or if customer adoption is slower than we anticipate, Agility’s ability to generate revenue and achieve profitability could be materially adversely affected. The robotics and warehouse automation industry is characterized by rapid technological change, evolving industry standards, and intensifying competition from a range of established and emerging players. If Agility is unable to keep pace with technological developments — including advances in machine learning, computer vision and bipedal locomotion — or to differentiate its Digit humanoid robot and future products effectively, its competitive position and operating results could be materially adversely affected. The robotics and warehouse automation industry is subject to rapid technological change, and Agility expects competition to intensify in the future. Agility’s product offerings compete in a broad competitive landscape that includes developers of humanoid robots, autonomous mobile robots, collaborative robots, fixed industrial automation systems, and traditional material -handling equipment. Agility also faces potential competition from diversified technology companies and robotic solution suppliers that do not have directly competing products today but could become competitors through organic development or acquisitions; such companies often have existing customer relationships and distribution channels that could enable them to emerge as formidable threats. Developments in alternative technologies, 29 Table of Contents such as advances in AI, machine learning, computer vision, and bipedal locomotion by competitors, may materially and adversely affect Agility’s business in ways it does not currently anticipate. Any failure by Agility to successfully react to changes in existing technologies or to develop new or enhanced technologies could materially harm its competitive position and growth prospects. Agility’s competitors may respond more quickly to new or emerging technologies, undertake more extensive marketing campaigns, have greater financial, manufacturing and other resources, or be more successful in attracting potential customers, employees and strategic partners. If Agility is not able to compete effectively, its business, prospects, financial condition and operating results will be negatively impacted. Competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying, including from well-funded market participants, many of which have significantly greater financial, technical and marketing resources than Agility. If these competitors bring competing humanoid and robotics products to market more quickly or at lower cost, or if they secure more favorable customer relationships, Agility’s competitiveness could be materially adversely affected. Competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well -funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems. Many of these competitors have significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources than Agility. They may be able to deploy greater resources to the design, development, manufacturing, distribution, promotion, sales, marketing, and support of their humanoid robotics programs. Additionally, these competitors may have longer operating histories, larger sales forces, broader customer and industry relationships, and other tangible and intangible resources that provide them with competitive advantages. Some competitors may decide to operate solely with a traditional sales model that may be viewed more favorably by potential customers, or may bundle their humanoid products with complementary offerings at lower effective prices. If any of these competitors bring competing humanoid products to market more quickly, at lower cost, with superior performance, or with more favorable customer terms, Agility’s competitiveness could be materially adversely affected. The market for humanoid robots designed to work alongside humans in warehouse, logistics and manufacturing environments is nascent and unproven. Important assumptions about the total addressable market for Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products, pricing under Agility’s Robots-as-a-Service subscription model (“RaaS”) and direct-sale models, customer adoption rates, and the length of sales and deployment cycles may prove to be inaccurate. If the market for humanoid robots does not develop as anticipated, or develops more slowly than expected, Agility’s business, financial condition, and results of operations would be materially and adversely affected. The market for humanoid robots designed to work alongside humans in warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing environments is nascent and largely unproven. Important assumptions about the total addressable market for Digit and future products, pricing under Agility’s RaaS subscription model and direct -sale models, customer adoption rates, anticipated future labor shortages and the length of sales and deployment cycles are based on management estimates that may prove inaccurate. Given the evolving nature of the markets in which Agility operates, it is difficult to predict customer demand or adoption rates for its products or the future growth of the markets it expects to target. If one or more of the targeted markets experience a shift in customer or prospective customer demand or new solutions that better address customer needs, Agility’s products may not compete as effectively, if at all. Agility’s expectations with respect to its total potential addressable market may differ from those of third parties, including investors or securities analysts. If demand does not develop as expected or if Agility cannot accurately forecast pricing, adoption rates, and sales cycle for its products, its business, results of operations, and financial condition will be adversely affected. The benefits offered by Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products could be supplanted by advances in competing technologies that may match or exceed the capabilities of humanoid robots at lower cost or with less operational complexity. If alternative automation technologies emerge that render humanoid robots less competitive or obsolete for warehouse, logistics and manufacturing applications, demand for Agility’s products could decline materially. The benefits offered by Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products could be supplanted by advances in autonomous mobile robots, fixed warehouse automation systems, AI -driven software solutions, or other competing technologies that may match or exceed the capabilities of humanoid robots at lower cost or with less operational complexity. Although Agility believes that its humanoid robots will be superior to alternative automation technologies in addressing tasks requiring human -like dexterity and mobility in unstructured environments, alternative technologies may match or exceed the benefits introduced by its products or be more cost effective. The development of any 30 Table of Contents alternative technology that can compete with or supplant humanoid robots may materially and adversely affect Agility’s business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results in ways Agility does not currently anticipate. Successful commercialization of competing automation approaches — including further advances in AMRs, AI -powered pick -and-place systems, or fully integrated warehouse automation platforms — may prove more cost effective or appealing to the warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing markets, potentially reducing market demand for Digit and future humanoid products. Any failure by Agility to develop new or enhanced technologies or processes, or to react to changes in existing technologies, could materially delay its development and introduction of new products, which could result in decreased revenue and a loss of market share. Adverse macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, rising interest rates, and tighter credit markets, could reduce customer capital spending on automation and robotics. During periods of economic uncertainty, Agility’s customers may delay, reduce, or cancel planned deployments of robotic systems, which would adversely affect Agility’s revenue, backlog, and growth prospects. Agility’s business is sensitive to general economic conditions and customer capital spending cycles. Adverse macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, rising interest rates, tighter credit markets, potential recession, and global trade uncertainty, could reduce customer capital spending on automation and robotics. During periods of economic uncertainty, customers in the warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing sectors may delay, reduce, or cancel planned deployments of robotic systems, extend evaluation and procurement timelines, or prioritize spending on core operations rather than new technology adoption. Agility’s RaaS subscription model, while designed to reduce customer upfront capital requirements, may still be viewed as discretionary spending during economic downturns. In addition, economic uncertainty may reduce the willingness of customers to commit to long -term subscription or deployment agreements. Any delay or reduction in customer spending would adversely affect Agility’s revenue, backlog, growth prospects, and ability to achieve profitability. Adoption of Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products in warehouse and logistics environments may be limited by employee resistance, organized labor concerns, and negative public perception regarding humanoid robots displacing human workers. Employee discomfort with or resistance to humanoid co-workers may be more pronounced with Digit as compared to conventional automation because Digit is designed to work alongside humans in shared workspaces, which could limit commercial acceptance and slow revenue growth. Even if Agility successfully markets its products, the purchase or subscription, adoption, and use of its humanoid robots may be materially and negatively impacted if the employees of Agility’s customers resist the use and adoption of the products. Agility’s customer’s employees may resist the adoption of humanoid robots for several reasons, including a perception that the benefit of using the products does not outweigh the perceived difficulties or discomfort associated with working alongside humanoid co -workers , resistance by labor unions, fear of job displacement, workplace discomfort with humanoid form factors, and safety concerns. Employee discomfort with or resistance to humanoid co -workers may be more pronounced with Digit than with conventional automation because Digit is designed to work alongside humans in shared workspaces and approximates human appearance and movement, which could create unease among workers. In addition, negative public perception regarding humanoid robots displacing human workers may lead to organized opposition, media criticism, political pressure or regulatory developments that constrain customer willingness to deploy Digit. If the employees of Agility’s customers resist adoption of Digit, or if negative public perception limits customer willingness to deploy humanoid robots, Agility’s business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results could be materially and adversely affected. Agility operates in an industry highly dependent on global supply chains for semiconductors, batteries, sensors, actuators, and specialty alloys. Disruptions to these supply chains — whether caused by geopolitical events, natural disasters, pandemics, or other factors — could delay production, increase costs, and materially impact Agility’s ability to fulfill customer orders on a timely basis. Agility relies on third -party suppliers for the provision and development of many key components and materials used in its products, including semiconductors, batteries, sensors, actuators, computing hardware, and specialty alloys. Some of the components used in Digit may have to be purchased from a single source or limited number of sources. If Agility’s suppliers are unable to supply key components and materials at the required volume, quality, or cost, Agility’s production schedules, sales, revenues, and profitability will likely be adversely affected. Agility and its suppliers may experience increases in the cost of and interruptions in the supply or shortage of materials due to geopolitical events, natural disasters, pandemics, trade restrictions, or other factors beyond Agility’s control. Due to 31 Table of Contents the complexity of its products, each Digit unit is expected to contain thousands of components, and difficulty securing any critical component could result in production delays that may be compounded if components require redesign or reengineering. Substantial increases in the prices for materials, such as battery cells, semiconductors, or specialty alloys, would increase Agility’s operating costs and could reduce its margins if the increased costs cannot be recouped through increased pricing. Any sustained supply interruption or shortage could prevent or delay the commercialization of Agility’s products and materially and negatively impact its business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results. Tariffs, trade restrictions, and ‘Buy American’ requirements may increase Agility’s costs or limit its ability to source critical components and sell into certain markets. Changes in trade policy or the imposition of new tariffs could disrupt Agility’s supply chain, raise input costs, and reduce the competitiveness of its products in both domestic and international markets. Agility is subject to risks relating to tariffs, trade restrictions, and government procurement requirements that may increase its costs or limit its ability to source critical components. The United States administration has imposed, and may continue to impose, tariffs on goods imported from other countries, and certain of these countries have imposed retaliatory tariffs. Changes in trade policy, the imposition of new tariffs, or the expansion of existing tariffs could increase the cost of components sourced internationally, disrupt established supply relationships, and reduce the competitiveness of Agility’s products in both domestic and international markets. In addition, ‘Buy American’ or other similar requirements imposed on government contractors may limit Agility’s ability to source components from the most cost -effective suppliers and may require Agility to establish domestic supply chains that are more expensive. If Agility cannot effectively mitigate the impact of tariffs and trade restrictions through alternative sourcing, supply chain restructuring, or other measures, its margins, production timelines, and competitive position could be materially adversely affected. Negative publicity, adverse events, product defects, or accidents involving competing humanoid robots or similar robotic products could harm public perception of the humanoid robotics market and adversely affect demand for Agility’s products. The humanoid robotics industry is in its early stages, and adverse events involving competitors’ products could harm public perception of the entire product category. High -profile accidents, product defects, malfunctions, or controversies involving humanoid robots or similar robotic products developed by Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, or other companies could damage public and customer confidence in humanoid robotics generally, regardless of whether such incidents involve Agility’s products. Because Agility operates in a new and evolving market, a single widely publicized safety incident — even one entirely unrelated to Agility — could set back industry -wide customer adoption and regulatory acceptance, result in new or more restrictive safety regulations, and reduce the willingness of warehouse, logistics, manufacturing, and other customers to deploy humanoid robots in their facilities. Negative media coverage or heightened regulatory scrutiny of humanoid robots as a category could reduce customer demand for Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and our other products by association, slow market adoption for all industry participants, and materially harm our business, reputation, and growth prospects. The market for humanoid and general-purpose robots is highly dependent on continued advances in AI, foundation models and computer vision, and Agility’s ability to integrate or develop competitive AI capabilities is critical to the performance and commercial viability of its humanoid robot, Digit, and future products. If the pace of AI development slows, if key AI technologies become unavailable or prohibitively expensive to license, or if competitors achieve superior AI integration, Agility’s products could become less competitive and its business could be materially adversely affected. The commercial viability of Agility’s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products is critically dependent on continued advances in AI, foundation models, and computer vision technologies. Agility relies on AI and machine learning capabilities to enable Digit to navigate complex warehouse environments, manipulate objects, and interact safely with human co -workers . If the pace of AI development slows, if key AI technologies become unavailable or prohibitively expensive to license, or if access to large -scale computing infrastructure necessary for AI model training becomes constrained, Agility’s ability to improve and maintain the performance of its products could be materially impaired. In addition, if competitors — including large technology companies with substantially greater resources — achieve superior AI integration in their humanoid or robotic products, Agility’s competitive position could be weakened. The Post-Closing Company’s ability to use Agility’s net operating losses and certain other tax attributes to offset future taxable income may be limited. Agility currently has substantial U.S. federal net operating loss (“ NOL ”) carry forward and other state tax attributes. The Post -Closing Company’s ability to use these tax attributes to reduce its future U.S. federal and state income tax obligations depends on many factors, including its future taxable income, the timing of which is uncertain. In addition, the use of these attributes may be subject to significant limitations under Section 382 and Section 383 of the Code, respectively, and similar provisions of state law, including limitations that may result from the consummation of the business combination. Under those sections of the Code, if a corporation undergoes an “ownership change,” the corporation’s ability to use its pre -change net operating loss carryforwards and other pre -change attributes, such as research tax credits, to offset its post -change income or tax may be limited. In general, an “ownership change” will occur if there is a cumulative change in ownership by “5 -percent shareholders” that exceeds 50 percentage points over a rolling three -year period. Similar rules may apply under state tax laws. Agility has not yet determined whether the business combination will give rise to an “ownership change” for purposes of Section 382 and Section 383 of the Code. Furthermore, Agility may have experienced ownership changes in the past and the Post -Closing Company may experience ownership changes in the future as a result of subsequent shifts in stock ownership (some of which shifts are outside of the Post -Closing Company’s control). As a result, the Post -Closing Company’s ability to use federal NOLs and other tax attributes to offset future taxable income and taxes could be subject to limitations. For these reasons, the Post -Closing Company may be unable to use a material portion of Agility’s NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect its future net income and cash flows. Agility’s business relies on AI technologies that are subject to a rapidly evolving and fragmented regulatory landscape across multiple jurisdictions, and failure to comply with new or changing AI laws could result in enforcement actions, significant fines, litigation, and restrictions on Agility’s ability to develop, deploy, or commercialize its products. We use AI and machine learning, including proprietary AI and machine learning algorithms and models, as well as third -party generative AI tools used internally to support software development and business operations (collectively, “AI Technologies”) throughout our business, and are making significant investments in this area. For example, we use AI Technologies to develop proprietary AI models that run onboard our robots to perform perception and motion control, and we use third -party generative AI tools internally to support software development and business operations. The regulatory framework for AI Technologies is rapidly evolving. Already, certain existing legal regimes (e.g., relating to data privacy) regulate certain aspects of AI Technologies, and many federal, state and foreign government bodies and agencies have enacted or are currently considering additional laws and regulations governing AI. Additionally, existing laws and regulations may be enjoined in judicial proceedings, or may be interpreted or enforced in ways that would affect the operation and use of our AI Technologies, or could be rescinded or amended as new administrations take differing approaches to evolving AI Technologies. As a result, implementation standards and enforcement practices are likely to remain uncertain for the foreseeable future, and we cannot predict the impact future laws, regulations, or standards, or the market perception of their requirements, may have on our business or how we will respond to these laws or regulations. In the United States, the regulatory framework for AI Technologies faces significant uncertainty. At the federal level, Congress has yet to enact meaningful AI legislation. Instead, federal policy on AI has been shaped by a series of executive orders that have shifted priorities and requirements substantially depending on the administration in power. In the absence of federal AI legislation, states have filled the void by enacting laws regulating different aspects of AI Technologies. For example, California has enacted laws and regulations related to AI safety protocols, reporting and transparency, among other AI -related topics. In addition, Utah’s Artificial Intelligence Policy Act establishes disclosure requirements and accountability measures for the use of generative AI in certain consumer interaction, and the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act prohibits the development and deployment of AI systems for certain purposes while establishing a regulatory sandbox. Numerous other states have enacted, passed, or are considering AI -focused legislation, creating a patchwork of regulations and a complex compliance challenge. However, the durability of these laws and the potential of additional state -level legislative activity faces uncertainty following President Trump’s December 2025 Executive Order “Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence.” This Executive Order establishes a federal policy favoring a uniform national AI regulatory framework designed to promote innovation and U.S. global competitiveness. The order directs federal agencies to identify, challenge, and potentially pre -empt state and local AI laws that are viewed as inconsistent with or burdensome to this national approach. It remains to be seen how agencies will effectuate this directive, and how states will approach AI legislation moving forward. Any or all of the foregoing regulatory developments could affect our use of AI and our ability to provide, improve or commercialize our services, require changes to our operations and processes, and materially adversely affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition. In Europe, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (the “ EU AI Act ”) has entered into force, and establishes a comprehensive, risk -based governance framework for AI in the EU market. Any failure by Agility to achieve or maintain compliance with applicable certifications or quality standards could result in regulatory enforcement, customer contract terminations, and reputational harm. New regulatory requirements that disproportionately affect humanoid robots — as compared to conventional automation — could reduce the economic value proposition of Agility’s products and limit market adoption. Agility must approach participation in the adoption of standards by industry standards bodies (such as the International Organization for Standardization, “ISO,” and the American National Standards Institute, “ANSI”) cautiously to ensure that none of its patents would be subject to such mandatory licensing obligations. Management may not be able to effectively and timely implement controls and procedures that adequately respond to the increased regulatory compliance and reporting requirements that will be applicable to the Post -Closing Company after the business combination. If the Post -Closing Company is not able to implement the requirements of Section 404, including any additional requirements once the Post -Closing Company is no longer an emerging growth company, in a timely manner or with adequate compliance, the Post -Closing Company may not be able to assess whether internal controls over financial reporting are effective, which may subject the Post -Closing Company to adverse regulatory consequences and could harm investor confidence and the market price of the Post -Closing Company’s common stock. The provisions of the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation requiring exclusive forum in the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware and the federal district courts of the United States for certain types of lawsuits may have the effect of discouraging certain lawsuits, including derivative lawsuits and lawsuits against our directors and officers, by limiting plaintiffs’ ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum that they find favorable. The Post -Closing Company’s proposed certificate of incorporation (the “ Proposed Certificate of Incorporation ”) provides that, to the fullest extent permitted by law, and unless the Post -Closing Company consents in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if and only if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware lacks subject Delaware) and any appellate court therefrom will be the sole and exclusive forum for (i) any derivative claim or cause of action brought on behalf of the Post -Closing Company, (ii) any claim or cause of action for breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any current or former director, officer or other employee of the Post -Closing Company to the Post -Closing Company or the Post -Closing Company’s stockholders, (iii) any claim or cause of action against the Post -Closing Company or any current or former director, officer or other employee of the Post -Closing Company arising out of or 64 Table of Contents pursuant to any provision of the DGCL or the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation or the Post -Closing Company’s proposed bylaws (the “ Proposed Bylaws ”), as either may be amended from time to time, (iv) any claim or cause of action seeking to interpret, apply, enforce or determine the validity of the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation or Proposed Bylaws, as either may be amended from time to time, (v) any claim or cause of action as to which the DGCL confers jurisdiction on the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware, or (vi) any claim or cause of action against the Post The Proposed Certificate of Incorporation also provides that, unless the Post -Closing Company consents in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the federal district courts of the United States shall be the exclusive forum for the resolution of any complaint asserting a cause of action arising under the Securities Act and the rules and regulations promulgated thereunder, including all causes of action asserted against any defendant to such complaint. Section 27 of the Exchange Act creates exclusive federal jurisdiction over all suits brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the Exchange Act or the rules and regulations thereunder. For the avoidance of doubt, this provision is intended to benefit and may be enforced by the Post -Closing Company, its officers and directors, the underwriter for any offering giving rise to such complaint and any other professional entity whose profession gives authority to a statement made by that person or entity and who has prepared or certified any part of the documents underlying the offering. These provisions may have the effect of discouraging certain lawsuits, including derivative lawsuits and lawsuits against directors and officers of the Post -Closing Company, by limiting plaintiffs’ ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum that they find favorable. The enforceability of similar choice of forum provisions in other companies’ certificates of incorporation or bylaws has been challenged in legal proceedings, and it is possible that, in connection with any applicable action brought against the Post -Closing Company, a court could find the choice of forum provisions contained in the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation to be inapplicable or unenforceable in such action. While the Delaware courts have determined that such choice of forum provisions are facially valid, a stockholder may nevertheless seek to bring a claim in a venue other than those designated in the exclusive forum provisions, and there can be no assurance that such provisions will be enforced by a court in those other jurisdictions. Investors cannot waive compliance with the federal securities laws and the rules and regulations thereunder. Following the business combination, the Post-Closing Company is expected to be an “emerging growth company” and a “smaller reporting company” within the meaning of the Securities Act, and to the extent that the Post-Closing Company takes advantage of certain exemptions from disclosure requirements available to emerging growth companies or smaller reporting companies, this could make the Post-Closing Company’s securities less attractive to investors and may make it more difficult to compare the Post-Closing Company’s performance with other public companies. Following the business combination, the Post -Closing Company is expected to be an “emerging growth company” within the meaning of the Securities Act, as modified by the JOBS Act, and the Post -Closing Company may take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not emerging growth companies including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes -Oxley Act, reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation in the Post -Closing Company’s periodic reports and proxy statements, and exemptions from the requirements of holding a nonbinding advisory vote on executive compensation and shareholder approval of any golden parachute payments not previously approved. As a result, the Post -Closing Company’s stockholders may not have access to certain information they may deem important. Neither CCXI nor Agility can predict whether investors will find the Post -Closing Company’s securities less attractive because the Post -Closing Company will rely on these exemptions. If some investors find the Post -Closing Company’s securities less attractive as a result of its reliance on these exemptions, the trading prices of the Post -Closing Company’s securities may be lower than they otherwise would be, there may be a less active trading market for the securities and the trading prices of the Post -Closing Company’s securities may be more volatile. Further, Section 102(b)(1) of the JOBS Act exempts emerging growth companies from being required to comply with new or revised financial accounting standards until private companies (that is, those that have not had a Securities Act registration statement declared effective or do not have a class of securities registered under the Exchange Act) are required to comply with the new or revised financial accounting standards. The JOBS Act provides that a company can elect to opt out of the extended transition period and comply with the requirements that apply to non -emerging growth 65 Table of Contents companies but any such election to opt out is irrevocable. CCXI has elected not to opt out of such extended transition period, which means that when a standard is issued or revised and it has different application dates for public or private companies, the Post -Closing Company as an emerging growth company, can adopt the new or revised standard at the time private companies adopt the new or revised standard. This may make comparison of the Post -Closing Company’s financial statements with another public company, which is neither an emerging growth company nor an emerging growth company which has opted out of using the extended transition period difficult or impossible because of the potential differences in accountant standards used. If the Post -Closing Company ceases to be an emerging growth company, the Post -Closing Company will no longer be able to take advantage of certain exemptions from reporting, and, absent other exemptions or relief available from the SEC, the Post -Closing Company will also be required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes -Oxley Act. The Post -Closing Company will incur additional expenses in connection with such compliance and the Post -Closing Company’s management will need to devote additional time and effort to implement and comply with such requirements. Additionally, after the business combination, the Post -Closing Company is expected to be a “smaller reporting company” as defined in Item 10(f)(1) of Regulation S -K . Smaller reporting companies may take advantage of certain reduced disclosure obligations, including, among other things, providing only two years of audited financial statements. The Post -Closing Company will remain a smaller reporting company until the last day of the fiscal year in which (1) the market value of the Post -Closing Company’s common stock held by non -affiliates equals or exceeds $250 million as of the end of that year’s second fiscal quarter, or (2) the Post -Closing Company’s annual revenues equaled or exceeded $100 million during such completed fiscal year or the market value of the Post -Closing Company’s common stock held by non -affiliates equals or exceeds $700 million as of the end of that year’s second fiscal quarter. To the extent that the Post -Closing Company takes advantage of such reduced disclosure obligations, it may also make comparison of the Post -Closing Company’s financial statements with other public companies difficult or impossible. Without consideration of the proposed business combination transaction, Agility has concluded there is substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern, which could materially adversely affect the Post-Closing Company’s business, financial condition, and the value of your investment. Agility’s historical financial statements have been prepared under the assumption that Agility will continue as a going concern. Agility has incurred operating losses since its inception and that management expects operating losses and negative cash flows to continue for the foreseeable future, which raises substantial doubt about Agility’s ability to continue as a going concern that Agility concluded could not be overcome by management’s plans as of the date of financials statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, which did not consider the proposed business combination transaction. In addition, Grant Thornton LLP, Agility’s independent registered public accounting firm, has issued a report on Agility’s audited financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024 that includes an explanatory paragraph stating that substantial doubt exists about Agility’s ability to continue as a going concern. The going concern basis of presentation assumes that, from the date the financial statements are issued, Agility will continue in operation, realize its assets and satisfy its liabilities in the normal course of business for a minimum of one year. Based on Agility’s current operating plan and forecasted cash flows, which did not consider the proposed business combination transaction, management has determined that existing cash and cash equivalents will not be sufficient to fund operations and satisfy obligations as they become due for at least one year from the date the financial statements are issued. Accordingly, substantial doubt exists regarding Agility’s ability to continue as a going concern within one year after the date the financial statements are issued. The accompanying financial statements do not include any adjustments relating to the recoverability and classification of recorded asset amounts or the amounts and classification of liabilities that might result from the outcome of this uncertainty. Agility is an early -stage growth company in the development stage that has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future. Agility has devoted substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot, Digit, and the build -out of its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, and has not yet generated sufficient revenue to offset its operating expenses. Agility has had negative cash flow from operating activities since inception, and expects to continue to have negative cash flow from operating and investing activities as it incurs research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative expenses, and makes capital expenditures in its efforts to increase sales and ramp up manufacturing operations. Management’s plans to alleviate these conditions include pursuing additional equity financing opportunities and strategic transactions, including the proposed business combination. During 2025, Agility completed multiple closings associated with its Series C financing and received aggregate net proceeds of approximately $162,385,117, and from January 1, 2026 through the date the financial statements were issued, received approximately $5,004,410 of additional proceeds associated with subsequent Series C closings. In addition, in July 2026, Agility raised $100 million of additional financing through the issuance and sale of simple agreements for future equity (“SAFEs”). However, the consummation of the proposed business combination is not fully within Agility’s control and are not considered probable of being effectively implemented under ASC 205 -40 , management has concluded that these plans do not alleviate the substantial doubt regarding Agility’s ability to continue as a going concern. The consummation of the business combination is expected to provide Agility with access to additional capital, which Agility expects will help fund its operations and business plan. However, there can be no assurance that the business combination will be completed or, if completed, that the proceeds therefrom will be sufficient to fund Agility’s operations for at least one year or to otherwise alleviate the conditions that raise substantial doubt about Agility’s ability to continue as a going concern. If Agility is not able to obtain additional equity or debt financing on reasonable terms, 68 Table of Contents or at all, or if the business combination is not consummated, Agility’s ability to fund its operations, continue its research and development activities, scale its manufacturing operations, and commercialize its products could be materially and adversely affected. The National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996, which is a federal statute, prevents or preempts the states from regulating the sale of certain securities, which are referred to as “covered securities.” Because CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares are listed on Nasdaq, CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares qualify as covered securities under such statute. Although the states are preempted from regulating the sale of CCXI securities, the federal statute does allow the states to investigate companies if there is a suspicion of fraud, and, if there is a finding of fraudulent activity, then the states can regulate or bar the sale of covered securities in a particular case. While CCXI is not aware of a state having used these powers to prohibit or restrict the sale of securities issued by blank check companies, other than the State of Idaho, certain state securities regulators view blank check companies unfavorably and might use these powers, or threaten to use these powers, to hinder the sale of securities of blank check companies in their states. Further, if CCXI were no longer listed on Nasdaq, CCXI’s securities would not qualify as covered securities under such statute and CCXI would be subject to regulation in each state in which CCXI offers CCXI’s securities.
