Because CCXI is incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands, in the event the business combination is not completed, you may face difficulties in protecting your interests, and your ability to protect your rights through the U.S. federal courts may be limited. Because CCXI is currently incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands, you may face difficulties in protecting your interests and your ability to protect your rights through the U.S. federal courts may be limited prior to the Domestication. CCXI is currently an exempted company under the laws of the Cayman Islands. As a result, it may be difficult for investors to effect service of process within the United States upon members of the CCXI Board or CCXI’s executive officers, or enforce judgments obtained in the U.S. courts against members of the CCXI Board or CCXI’s officers. Until the Domestication is effected, CCXI’s corporate affairs are governed by the CCXI current articles of association, the Companies Act and the common law of the Cayman Islands. CCXI is also subject to the federal securities laws of the United States. The rights of shareholders to take action against members of the CCXI Board, actions by minority shareholders and the fiduciary responsibilities of members of the CCXI Board to CCXI under the laws of the Cayman Islands are to a large extent governed by the common law of the Cayman Islands. The common law in the Cayman Islands is derived in part from comparatively limited judicial precedent in the Cayman Islands and from English common law. Appeals from the Cayman Islands Courts to the Privy Council (which is the final Court of Appeal for British overseas territories such as the Cayman Islands) are binding on a court in the Cayman Islands. Decisions of the English courts, and particularly the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeal are generally of persuasive authority but are not binding in the courts of the Cayman Islands. Decisions of courts in other Commonwealth jurisdictions are similarly of persuasive but not binding authority. The rights of CCXI’s shareholders and the fiduciary responsibilities of members of the CCXI Board under Cayman Islands law are different from what they would be under statutes or judicial precedent in some jurisdictions in the United States. In particular, the Cayman Islands has a different body of securities laws as compared to the United States, and certain states, such as Delaware, may have more fully developed and judicially interpreted bodies of corporate law. In addition, Cayman Islands companies may not have standing to initiate a shareholders derivative action in a federal court of the United States. CCXI has been advised by Ogier (Cayman) LLP, its Cayman Islands legal counsel, that the courts of the Cayman Islands are unlikely (1) to recognize or enforce against CCXI judgments of courts of the United States predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the United States or any state; and (2) in original actions brought in the Cayman Islands, to impose liabilities against CCXI predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the United States or any state, so far as the liabilities imposed by those provisions are penal in nature. In those circumstances, although there is no statutory enforcement in the Cayman Islands of judgments obtained in the United States, the courts of the Cayman Islands will recognize and enforce a foreign money judgment of a foreign court of competent jurisdiction without retrial on the merits based on the principle that a judgment of a competent foreign court imposes upon the judgment debtor an obligation to pay the sum for which judgment has been given provided certain conditions are met. For a foreign judgment to be enforced in the Cayman Islands, such judgment must be final and conclusive and for a liquidated sum, and must not be in respect of taxes or a fine or penalty, inconsistent with a Cayman Islands judgment in respect of the same matter, impeachable on the grounds of fraud or obtained in a manner, or be of a kind the enforcement of which is, contrary to natural justice or the public policy of the Cayman Islands (awards of punitive or multiple damages may well be held to be contrary to public policy). A Cayman Islands court may stay enforcement proceedings if concurrent proceedings are being brought elsewhere. 74 Table of Contents As a result of the above, the public shareholders may have more difficulty in protecting their interests in the face of actions taken by CCXI’s executive officers, members of the CCXI Board or controlling shareholders than they would as public shareholders of a U.S. company. The Domestication may result in adverse tax consequences for holders of CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants. CCXI intends for the Domestication to qualify as a reorganization within the meaning of Section 36 8(a)(1)(F) of the Code, i.e., an F Reorganization (and is not otherwise treated as a reorganization within the meaning of Section 368(a)(1) of the Code). If the Domestication fails to qualify as an F Reorganization (and does not otherwise qualify as a “reorganization” within the meaning of Section 368(a) of the Code), a U.S. Holder generally would recognize gain or loss with respect to its CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants in an amount equal to the difference, if any, between the sum of the fair market value of the corresponding CCXI common stock or CCXI Warrants received in the Domestication and the U.S. Holder’s adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants surrendered. U.S. Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication. Additionally, Non -U .S. Holders generally will become subject to withholding tax on any amounts treated as dividends paid on Agility common stock after the Domestication. Assuming that the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, subject to the PFIC rules discussed below, U.S. Holders generally will be subject to Section 367(b) of the Code in connection with the Domestication, and, as a result: • a U.S. Holder who is a 10% U.S. Shareholder on the date of the Domestication generally will be required to include in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI the “all earnings and profits amount” (as defined in the Treasury Regulations under Section 367(b) of the Code) attributable to the CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares held directly by such U.S. Holder; • a U.S. Holder whose CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares have a fair market value of $50,000 or more on the date of the Domestication and who, on the date of the Domestication, is not a 10% U.S. Shareholder generally will recognize gain (but not loss) with respect to its CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares as if such U.S. Holder exchanged its CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares for CCXI common stock in a taxable transaction, unless such U.S. Holder elects in accordance with applicable Treasury Regulations to include in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI the “all earnings and profits amount” (as defined in the Treasury Regulations under Section 367(b) of the Code) attributable to such U.S. Holder’s CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares; and • a U.S. Holder whose CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares have a fair market value of less than $50,000 on the date of the Domestication and who, on the date of the Domestication, is not a 10% U.S. Shareholder, generally will not recognize any gain or loss or include any part of CCXI’s earnings and profits in income under Section 367 of the Code in connection with the Domestication. Additionally, even if the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, proposed Treasury Regulations promulgated under Section 1291(f) of the Code and certain other PFIC rules (which have retroactive proposed effective dates) generally require that a U.S. person who disposes of stock of a PFIC (including for this purpose, under a proposed Treasury Regulation that generally treats an “option” to acquire the stock of a PFIC as stock of the PFIC, exchanging CCXI Warrants for newly issued CCXI Delaware Warrants in the Domestication) must recognize gain equal to the excess of the fair market value of such PFIC stock over its adjusted tax basis, notwithstanding any other provision of the Code. CCXI believes that it is likely classified as a PFIC for U.S. federal income tax purposes. As a result, these proposed Treasury Regulations, if finalized in their current form, would generally require a U.S. Holder of CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares to recognize gain under the PFIC rules on the exchange of CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares for CCXI common stock pursuant to the Domestication unless such U.S. Holder has made certain tax elections with respect to such U.S. Holder’s CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares. The proposed Treasury Regulations provide coordinating rules with other sections of the Code, including Section 367(b), which affect the manner in which the rules under such other sections apply to transfers of PFIC stock. These proposed Treasury Regulations, if finalized in their current form, would also apply to a U.S. Holder who exchanges CCXI Warrants for newly issued CCXI Delaware Warrants; under current law, however, the elections mentioned above do not apply to CCXI Warrants. Any gain recognized from the application of the PFIC rules described above would be taxable income with no corresponding receipt of cash. The tax on any such gain would be imposed at the rate applicable to ordinary income and an interest charge would apply based on complex rules designed to offset the tax deferral to such U.S. Holder on the undistributed earnings, 75 Table of Contents if any, of CCXI. It is not possible to determine at this time whether, in what form, and with what effective date, final Treasury Regulations under Section 1291(f) of the Code may be adopted or how any such Treasury Regulations would apply. The CCXI public warrant agreement designates the courts of the State of New York or the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York as the sole and exclusive forum for certain types of actions and proceedings that may be initiated by holders of CCXI warrants, which could limit the ability of CCXI warrantholders to obtain a favorable judicial forum for disputes with CCXI. The CCXI warrant agreement provides that, subject to applicable law, (i) any action, proceeding or claim against CCXI arising out of or relating in any way to the warrant agreement, including under the Securities Act, will be brought and enforced in the courts of the State of New York or the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, and (ii) that CCXI irrevocably submits to such jurisdiction, which jurisdiction shall be the exclusive forum for any such action, proceeding or claim. CCXI will waive any objection to such exclusive jurisdiction and that such 78 Table of Contents courts represent an inconvenient forum. CCXI notes, however, that there is uncertainty as to whether a court would enforce this provision and that investors cannot waive compliance with the federal securities laws and the rules and regulations thereunder. Section 22 of the Securities Act creates concurrent jurisdiction for state and federal courts over all suits brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the Securities Act or the rules and regulations thereunder. Notwithstanding the foregoing, these provisions of the CCXI public warrant agreement do not apply to suits brought to enforce any liability or duty created by the Exchange Act or any other claim for which the district courts of the United States of America are the sole and exclusive forum. Any person or entity purchasing or otherwise acquiring any interest in any of the CCXI public warrants shall be deemed to have notice of and to have consented to the forum provisions in the CCXI public warrant agreement. If any action, the subject matter of which is within the scope of the forum provisions of the CCXI public warrant agreement is filed in a court other than a court of the State of New York located in the County of New York or the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (a “ foreign action ”) in the name of any holder of the CCXI public warrants, such holder shall be deemed to have consented to: (x) the personal jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in the State of New York in connection with any action brought in any such court to enforce the forum provisions, and (y) having service of process made upon such warrantholder in any such action brought in such court to enforce the forum provisions by service upon such warrantholder’s counsel in the foreign action as agent for such warrantholder. This choice -of-forum provision may limit a warrantholder’s ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum that it finds favorable for disputes with CCXI, which may discourage such lawsuits. Warrantholders who are unable to bring their claims in the judicial forum of their choosing may be required to incur additional costs in pursuit of actions which are subject to CCXI’s choice -of-forum provisions. Alternatively, if a court were to find this provision of CCXI’s public warrant agreement inapplicable or unenforceable with respect to one or more of the specified types of actions or proceedings, CCXI may incur additional costs associated with resolving such matters in other jurisdictions, which could materially and adversely affect CCXI’s business, financial condition and results of operations and result in a diversion of the time and resources of CCXI’s management and board of directors. CFIUS or other regulatory agencies may modify, delay or prevent the business combination. CFIUS has authority to review direct and indirect foreign acquisitions of and certain foreign investments in U.S. businesses. Whether CFIUS has jurisdiction to review a transaction depends on, among other factors, the nature and structure of the transaction (including the level of the foreign counterparty’s beneficial ownership interest and the nature of the foreign counterparty’s information or governance rights with respect to the U.S. business), and the nature of the U.S. business’s technology and operations (e.g., data collection practices). 81 Table of Contents All transactions that could result in foreign “control” of a U.S. business as that term is defined in the CFIUS regulations are subject to CFIUS jurisdiction. Transactions with foreign counterparties involving a U.S. businesses that has a qualifying nexus to “critical technology,” “critical infrastructure,” or “sensitive personal data” are subject to a lower CFIUS jurisdiction threshold that is triggered when a foreign investor will not “control” the U.S. business, but will be afforded certain information or governance rights with respect to the U.S. business — including board representation or observer rights, access to certain nonpublic technical information, or the right to involvement in certain company decision making. When a foreign acquisition or investment transaction is subject to CFIUS jurisdiction (a “ Covered Transaction ”), the CFIUS regulations may require the parties thereto to submit pre -closing filings seeking CFIUS approval to close the transaction at issue. In the absence of such “mandatory” filing requirements, and if the parties forego a “voluntary” CFIUS filing, CFIUS may initiate a review of the covered transaction post -closing on its own initiative. If during the course of a review of a covered transaction CFIUS determines that the transaction gives rise to national security concerns, CFIUS may prohibit, unwind, or place restrictions on the transaction. If the business combination were to fall within CFIUS’s jurisdiction, CFIUS may inquire about, intervene in, prohibit, or unwind the transaction or parts thereof before or after the closing. For example, CFIUS may decide to modify the transaction by limiting certain foreign shareholder rights, or to delay the business combination to address perceived national security concerns therewith. If CFIUS determines that it is unable to address perceived national security issues with the transaction by modifying the terms thereof, CFIUS may request the President of the United States to prohibit the business combination before closing, or unwind the transaction or parts thereof after closing — including by requiring certain foreign investors to divest of some or all of their ownership interest in CCXI. Should CFIUS inquire about the business combination or require a formal review thereof, the time necessary for the completion of such inquiry or review may prevent the business combination from occurring within the applicable time period required under CCXI’s certificate of incorporation. These risks may limit the attractiveness of, delay or prevent CCXI from pursuing the business combination. Any foreign direct investment regulatory review, whether by CFIUS or otherwise, could be lengthy, and CCXI has limited time to complete the business combination. CCXI’s business is to identify and complete a business combination and thereafter to operate the post -transaction business or assets for the long term. CCXI does not plan to buy businesses or assets with a view to resale or profit from their resale. CCXI does not plan to buy unrelated businesses or assets or to be a passive investor. Pursuant to the trust agreement, the trustee is not permitted to invest in other securities or assets. By restricting the investment of the proceeds to these instruments and by subsequently holding all funds in the trust account in cash, which may include demand deposit accounts (as described in the following paragraph), and by having a business plan targeted at acquiring and growing businesses for the long -term (rather than on buying and selling businesses in the manner of a merchant bank or private equity fund), CCXI does not believe CCXI is an “investment company” within the meaning of the Investment Company Act. The CCXI IPO was not intended for persons seeking a return on investments in government securities or investment securities. The trust account is intended as a holding place for funds pending the earliest to occur of: (1) the completion of CCXI’s primary business objective, which is a business combination; (2) the redemption of any public shares properly submitted in connection with a shareholder vote to amend the CCXI current articles of association (a) to modify the substance or timing of CCXI’s obligation to redeem 100% of the public shares if CCXI has not consummated an initial business combination within the completion window, or (b) with respect to any other provision of the articles relating to the rights of holders of CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares or pre -initial business combination activity; and (3) the redemption of CCXI’s public shares if CCXI has not completed an initial business combination within the completion window. Because CCXI has invested only in permitted instruments, CCXI believes CCXI is not an investment company. If CCXI is deemed to be subject to the Investment Company Act, compliance with these additional regulatory burdens would require additional expenses for which CCXI has not allotted funds and may hinder CCXI’s ability to consummate CCXI’s initial business combination. If CCXI is unable to complete the initial business combination within the completion window CCXI’s public shareholders may receive only approximately $10.00 per share on the liquidation of CCXI’s trust account. In certain circumstances, CCXI’s public shareholders may receive less than $10.00 per share on the redemption of their shares if CCXI is unable to complete CCXI’s initial business combination within the completion window. To mitigate the risk of being deemed to have been operating as an unregistered investment company (including under the subjective test of Section 3(a)(1)(A) of the Investment Company Act of 1940, as amended), all funds in the trust account are held and will be held in cash (which may include demand deposit accounts) until the earlier of consummation of CCXI’s initial business combination or liquidation. Furthermore, such cash (which may include demand deposit accounts) is held in bank accounts that exceed federally insured limits as guaranteed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the “ FDIC ”). While CCXI has only placed CCXI’s trust account deposits with Continental Stock Transfer & Trust Company, only a small portion of the funds in CCXI’s trust account will be guaranteed by the FDIC. 86 Table of Contents The Post-Closing Company may be subject to a 1% U.S. federal excise tax in connection with redemptions of the Post-Closing Company common stock. On August 16, 2022, President Biden signed into law the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which, among other things, imposes a 1% excise tax on the fair market value of stock repurchased by “covered corporations” beginning in 2023, with certain exceptions (the “ Excise Tax ”). The Excise Tax is imposed on the repurchasing corporation itself, not its stockholders from whom or which the stock is repurchased. Because the Post -Closing Company is domesticating and continuing as a Delaware corporation and CCXI’s securities will continue to trade on Nasdaq, we believe that we are a “covered corporation” for this purpose, however, we expect that we will not be subject to material excise tax payments in connection with redemptions, either because redemptions will occur prior to the Domestication or because such redemptions will be offset by other share issuances made by us during the same taxable year. The amount of the Excise Tax is generally 1% of the fair market value of the shares repurchased at the time of the repurchase. However, for purposes of calculating the Excise Tax, repurchasing corporations are permitted to net the fair market value of certain new stock issuances (such as the shares of Post -Closing Company common stock being issued in the business combination) against the fair market value of stock repurchases during the same taxable year. In addition, certain exceptions apply to the Excise Tax. Any redemption or other repurchase that the Post -Closing Company makes after the Domestication may be subject to the Excise Tax. Whether and to what extent the Post -Closing Company would be subject to the Excise Tax would depend on a number of factors, including (1) the fair market value of the redemptions and repurchases in connection with the business combination, (2) the nature and amount of any equity issuances in connection with the business combination, including the business combination and any PIPE Investment, and (3) the content of regulations and other guidance from the U.S. Department of Treasury. Prior to the consummation of the business combination, funds in the trust account, including any interest thereon, will not be used to pay for any Excise Tax. If the business combination is consummated, any Excise Taxes from redemptions of shares of CCXI public shares in connection with the business combination would reduce the funds available to Agility for working capital following the business combination. If the Merger does not qualify as a “reorganization” for U.S. federal income tax purposes, Agility U.S. Holders will be required to recognize gain or loss for U.S. federal income tax purposes upon the exchange of their Agility common stock for Post-Closing Company common stock in the Merger. The U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Merger to Agility U.S. Holders generally will depend on whether the Merger qualifies as a “reorganization” for U.S. federal income tax purposes. If the Merger fails to qualify as a reorganization within the meaning of Section 368(a) of the Code, an Agility U.S. Holder generally would recognize gain or loss for U.S. federal income tax purposes on each share of Agility capital stock surrendered in the Merger for Post -Closing Company common stock. For a more complete discussion of the material U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Merger, please carefully review the information set forth in the section entitled “ Material U.S. Federal Income Tax Considerations of the Merger ” in this proxy statement/prospectus. Each Agility U.S. Holder should consult its own tax advisor to determine the particular tax consequences to it in light of its own particular circumstances if the Merger fails to qualify as a reorganization for U.S. federal income tax purposes. Risks Related to the Redemption You must tender your CCXI public shares in order to validly exercise your redemption rights. In connection with tendering your shares for redemption, you must request in writing that CCXI redeem your CCXI public shares for cash and elect either to physically tender your share certificates to CCXI’s transfer agent or to deliver your shares to the transfer agent electronically using The Depository Trust Company’s DWAC System, which election would likely be determined based on the manner in which you hold your shares, in each case, by two business days prior to the initially scheduled vote on the business combination proposal or such later date as CCXI’s directors may determine. The requirement for physical or electronic delivery by two business days prior to the initially scheduled vote on the business combination proposal or such later date as CCXI’s directors may determine ensures that a redeeming holder’s election to redeem is irrevocable once the business combination is approved. Any failure to observe these procedures will result in your loss of redemption rights in connection with the vote on the business combination. CCXI does not have a specified maximum redemption threshold. The absence of such a redemption 87 Table of Contents threshold may make it possible for CCXI to complete a business combination with which a substantial majority of CCXI’s shareholders do not agree. The CCXI current articles of association does not provide a specified maximum redemption threshold. CCXI will not redeem public shares in an amount that would cause CCXI’s net tangible assets to be less than $5,000,001 (as determined in accordance with Rule 3a51 -1 (g)(1) of the Exchange Act). As a result, CCXI may be able to complete the business combination even though a substantial portion of public shareholders do not agree with the transaction and have redeemed their shares or have entered into privately negotiated agreements to sell their shares to the Sponsor, directors or officers or their affiliates. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, except for the Sponsor Agreement, no agreements with respect to the private purchase of public shares by CCXI or the persons described above have been entered into with any such investor or holder. CCXI will file a Current Report on Form 8 -K with the SEC to disclose private arrangements entered into or significant private purchases made by any of the aforementioned persons that would affect the vote on the business combination proposal or other proposals (as described in this proxy statement/prospectus) at the extraordinary general meeting. For more information regarding the Sponsor Agreement, please see the section entitled “ Proposal No. 1 — The Business Combination Proposal — Certain Agreements Related to the Business Combination — Sponsor Agreement. ” In the event that the aggregate cash consideration that CCXI would be required to pay for all shares of CCXI public shares that are validly submitted for redemption, plus any amount required to satisfy the foregoing cash condition pursuant to the terms of the Merger Agreement, exceeds the aggregate amount of cash available to CCXI, CCXI may not complete the business combination or redeem any shares, and all shares of CCXI public shares submitted for redemption will be returned to the holders thereof and CCXI may instead search for an alternate business combination. Public shareholders, together with any affiliates of theirs or any other person with whom they are acting in concert or as a “group,” will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the public shares. The CCXI current articles of association provides that a public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such shareholders or any other person with whom such stockholder is acting in concert or as a “group” (as defined under Section 13(d) of the Exchange Act), will be restricted from redeeming in the aggregate his, her or its shares or, if part of such a group, the group’s shares, in excess of 15% of the CCXI public shares unless such shareholder first obtains CCXI’s prior consent (the “ Excess Shares ”). Your inability to redeem Excess Shares will reduce your influence over CCXI’s ability to consummate the business combination and you could suffer a material loss on your investment in CCXI if you sell such excess shares in open market transactions. Additionally, you will not receive redemption distributions with respect to such excess shares if CCXI consummates the business combination. As a result, you will continue to hold that number of shares aggregating to more than 15% of the shares sold in the CCXI IPO and, in order to dispose of such excess shares, would be required to sell your shares in open market transactions, potentially at a loss. CCXI cannot assure you that the value of such excess shares will appreciate over time following the business combination or that the market price of CCXI public shares will exceed the per share redemption price. Notwithstanding the foregoing, shareholders may challenge CCXI’s determination as to whether a shareholder is acting in concert or as a group with another shareholder in a court of competent jurisdiction. However, CCXI’s shareholders’ ability to vote all of their shares (including Excess Shares) for or against the business combination is not restricted by this limitation on redemption. There is no guarantee that a shareholder’s decision whether to redeem its shares for a pro rata portion of the trust account will put the shareholder in a better future economic position. CCXI can give no assurance as to the price at which a shareholder may be able to sell its public shares in the future following the completion of the business combination or any alternative business combination. Certain events following the consummation of any initial business combination, including the business combination, may cause an increase in CCXI’s share price, and may result in a lower value realized now than a shareholder of CCXI might realize in the future had the shareholder not redeemed its shares. Similarly, if a shareholder does not redeem its shares, the shareholder will bear the risk of ownership of the public shares after the consummation of any initial business combination, and there can be no assurance that a shareholder can sell its shares in the future for a greater amount than the redemption price set forth in this proxy statement/prospectus. A shareholder should consult the shareholder’s own tax and/or financial advisor for assistance on how this may affect his, her or its individual situation. 88 Table of Contents Shareholders of CCXI who wish to redeem their CCXI public shares for a pro rata portion of the trust account must comply with specific requirements for redemption that may make it more difficult for them to exercise their redemption rights prior to the deadline. Risks if the Adjournment Proposal Is Not Approved If the adjournment proposal is not approved, and an insufficient number of votes have been obtained to authorize the consummation of the business combination, the CCXI Board will not have the ability to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date in order to solicit further votes, and, therefore, the business combination will not be approved. If, at the extraordinary general meeting, the CCXI Board determines that it would be in the best interest of CCXI to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to give CCXI more time to consummate the business combination for whatever reason (such as if the business combination proposal is not approved, or if additional time is needed to fulfill other closing conditions), the CCXI Board will seek approval to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date or dates. If the adjournment proposal is not approved, the CCXI Board will not have the ability to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date and, therefore, the business combination would not be completed. 89 Table of Contents DILUTION Unless the context otherwise requires, references in this subsection to “we,” “our” and “us” generally refer to CCXI prior to the business combination. On the CCXI record date, there were 55,700,000 CCXI Ordinary Shares outstanding, of which 41,900,000 were CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares and 13,800,000 were CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares. Quorum A quorum of CCXI shareholders is necessary to hold a valid meeting. A quorum for such meeting will consist of the holders present by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy of CCXI Ordinary Shares representing at least one -third (1/3) of the paid up voting share capital of CCXI entitled to vote at such meeting. The Sponsor owns            % of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares (            % of the outstanding CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares and            % of the outstanding CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date, which will count towards this quorum. As a result, as of the CCXI record date, in addition to shares of the Sponsor,            CCXI Ordinary Shares held by CCXI public shareholders would be required to be present at the extraordinary general meeting to achieve a quorum. Proxies that are marked “abstain” will be treated as shares of CCXI public shares present for purposes of determining the presence of a quorum on all matters. Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. Effect of Abstentions and Broker Non-Votes As a matter of Cayman Islands law, abstentions will not constitute votes cast at the CCXI extraordinary general meeting and therefore will have no effect on the approval of the proposals. Under the rules of various national and regional securities exchanges, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to nonroutine matters unless you provide instructions on how to vote in accordance with the information and procedures provided to you by your broker, bank or nominee. We believe the proposals presented to the shareholders at the extraordinary general meeting will be considered nonroutine and, therefore, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares without your instruction on any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. If you do not provide voting instructions to your broker, bank or other nominee with respect to any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting, your broker, bank or other nominee may deliver a proxy card expressly indicating that it is NOT voting your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to those proposals; this indication that a broker, bank or nominee is not voting your shares is referred to as a “broker non -vote .” Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. Your bank, broker or other nominee can vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares only if you provide instructions on how to vote. You should instruct your broker to vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares in accordance with directions you provide. Broker non -votes will not have any effect on the outcome of the proposals. Vote Required for Approval The Sponsor owns of record and is entitled to vote % of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares ( % of the outstanding CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares and % of the outstanding CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date. Such shares, as well as any CCXI Ordinary Shares acquired in the aftermarket by the Sponsor, will be voted in favor of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. Accordingly, the business combination proposal does not require the approval of a majority of the unaffiliated holders of CCXI. 96 Table of Contents The approval of each of the business combination proposal, stock issuance proposal, incentive plan proposal, ESPP proposal, director election proposal, advisory organizational documents proposal, and, if necessary, the adjournment proposal requires an ordinary resolution, being the affirmative vote of a simple majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder’s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the business combination proposal, stock issuance proposal, incentive plan proposal, ESPP proposal, director election proposal and, if necessary, the adjournment proposal, will have no effect on such proposals. Prior to the closing of an initial business combination, the CCXI current articles of association prescribe that only holders of CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares are entitled to appoint and remove directors. This provision of the CCXI current articles of association may only be amended if approved by a special resolution passed by at least 90% (or, where such amendment is proposed in respect of the consummation of CCXI’s initial business combination, two -thirds ) of the CCXI Ordinary Shares voting at the applicable general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, the director election proposal is being voted on by CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only. The approval of the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal requires a special resolution, being the affirmative vote of holders of at least two -thirds of the CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder’s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal will have no effect on such proposals. Under the CCXI current articles of association, CCXI’s directors have the authority to resolve that CCXI be registered by way of continuation in a jurisdiction outside the Cayman Islands or such other jurisdiction in which it is for the time being incorporated, registered or existing (including, but not limited to, the approval of the organizational documents to be adopted by the Company in such other jurisdiction to the extent applicable). Accordingly, it is not necessary for CCXI to receive shareholder consent to the domestication, and the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal are therefore being presented to CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only. Consummation of the business combination is conditioned on the approval of each of the condition precedent proposals. If any of those proposals are not approved, at the extraordinary general meeting (or any adjournment or postponement thereof) then unless certain conditions in the Merger Agreement are waived by the applicable parties to the Merger Agreement, the Merger Agreement may be terminated and the business combination may not be consummated. Redemption Rights Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, any holder of CCXI public shares who is not the Sponsor or a CCXI officer or director may, contemporaneously with the vote on the business combination proposal, request to redeem all or a portion of its CCXI public shares for cash, regardless of whether it votes “for” or “against” the business combination proposal. Any such CCXI shareholder holding CCXI public shares as of the CCXI record date may demand that CCXI redeem such shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals (which, for illustrative purposes, was approximately $ per share as of the CCXI record date), calculated as of two business days prior to the anticipated consummation of the business combination. If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises its redemption rights as described in this section and the business combination is consummated, CCXI will redeem such holder’s shares for a pro rata portion of funds held in the trust account and the holder will no longer own CCXI public shares following the business combination. Notwithstanding the foregoing, (1) a holder of CCXI public shares, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a “group” (as defined in Section 13(d)(3) of the Exchange Act), will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the CCXI public shares. Accordingly, all CCXI public shares in excess of 15% held by a CCXI public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a “group,” will not be redeemed for cash and (2) a holder of CCXI public shares that holds CCXI public shares beneficially through a nominee must identify itself to CCXI in connection with any redemption election in order to validly redeem such CCXI public shares. Moreover, pursuant to the terms of the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have each agreed to waive any redemption rights with respect to any CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares they own in connection with the consummation of the business combination. Holders of CCXI public shares may demand redemption by delivering their shares, either physically or electronically using Depository Trust Company’s DWAC System, and requesting in writing that CCXI redeem such CCXI public shares for cash to Continental Stock Transfer & Trust Company, CCXI’s transfer agent, at least two business days prior to the initially scheduled vote at the extraordinary general meeting (the “ Redemption Deadline ”). If you hold the shares of CCXI in street name, you will have to coordinate with your broker to have your shares certificated or delivered electronically. Certificates that have not been tendered (either physically or electronically) in accordance with these procedures will not be redeemed for cash. There is a nominal cost associated with this tendering process and the act of certificating the shares of CCXI public shares or delivering them through the DWAC System. The transfer 98 Table of Contents agent will typically charge the tendering broker $100 and it would be up to the broker whether or not to pass this cost on to the redeeming shareholder. In the event the business combination is not consummated, this may result in an additional cost to CCXI shareholders for the return of their shares. The Redemption Deadline may occur prior to the Domestication, but the redemption will be with respect to Post -Closing Company common stock that an electing holder of CCXI public shares holds after the Domestication. For the purposes of the CCXI current articles of association, the exercise of redemption rights will be treated as an election to have such CCXI public shares redeemed for cash, and references in this proxy statement/prospectus to “redemption” or “redeeming” will be interpreted accordingly. Immediately following the Domestication and the Closing, the Post -Closing Company will satisfy the exercise of redemption rights by redeeming the corresponding shares of Post -Closing Company common stock issued to the CCXI public shareholders that validly exercised their redemption rights. If the business combination is not approved or completed for any reason, then holders of CCXI public shares that elected to exercise their redemption rights will not be entitled to redeem their CCXI public shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account, as applicable. In such case, CCXI will promptly return any CCXI public shares delivered by shareholders. The closing price of CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares on the CCXI record date was $ per share. The cash held in the trust account on such date was approximately $ ($ per CCXI public share outstanding as of the record date). Prior to exercising redemption rights, CCXI shareholders should verify the market price of CCXI public shares as they may receive higher proceeds from the sale of their shares in the public market than from exercising their redemption rights if the market price per share is higher than the redemption price. CCXI cannot assure its shareholders that they will be able to sell their CCXI public shares in the open market, even if the market price per share is higher than the redemption price stated above, as there may not be sufficient liquidity in its securities when CCXI shareholders wish to sell their shares. If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises their redemption rights and the business combination is consummated, then they will be exchanging their CCXI public shares for cash and will no longer own those shares. They will be entitled to receive cash for their CCXI public shares only if they properly exercise their redemption rights no later than the Redemption Deadline by delivering their share certificate (either physically or electronically) to CCXI’s transfer agent prior to the Redemption Deadline. Pursuant to the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have agreed to waive their redemption rights with respect to all of their CCXI Ordinary Shares in connection with the consummation of the business combination and, because of this, such CCXI Ordinary Shares are excluded from the pro rata calculation used to determine the per share redemption price. As is customary in transactions of this type, the Sponsor and the Insiders did not receive any consideration for waiving their redemption rights. Such a purchase may include a contractual acknowledgement that such shareholder, although still the record holder of our shares, is no longer the beneficial owner thereof and therefore agrees not to exercise its redemption rights. In the event shares are purchased in privately negotiated transactions from public shareholders who have already elected to exercise their redemption rights, such selling shareholders would be required to revoke their prior elections to redeem their shares. The purpose of such purchases would be to reduce the number of shares of CCXI public shares that may be redeemed in connection with the business combination, and may include a business decision to increase such purchaser’s ownership at an attractive price. In addition, the Sponsor and/or its affiliates may purchase CCXI public shares on the open market prior to the extraordinary general meeting and separate from the redemption process conducted in connection with the business combination (“ Open Market Purchases ”). The Sponsor and/or its respective affiliates shall only make Open Market Purchases to the extent the price per share of CCXI public shares so acquired is no higher than the redemption price that would be available in connection with the redemption procedures described in this proxy statement/prospectus. In addition, the Sponsor and/or its affiliates will waive any redemption rights with respect to any CCXI public shares purchased in Open Market Purchases and will not vote any CCXI public shares purchased in Open Market Purchases in favor of the proposals. While the exact nature of any such arrangements has not been determined as of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, they might include, without limitation, arrangements to protect such investors or holders against potential loss in value of their shares, including the granting of put options and, with Agility’s consent, the transfer to such investors or holders of shares owned by the Sponsor for nominal value. Entering into any such arrangements may have a negative effect on the market price of CCXI Ordinary Shares. For example, as a result of these arrangements, an investor or holder may have the ability to effectively purchase shares at a price lower than market and may therefore be more likely to sell the shares such person owns, either prior to or immediately after the extraordinary general meeting. If such transactions are effected, the consequence could be to cause the business combination to be approved in circumstances where such approval could not otherwise be obtained. 114 Table of Contents • by Agility if the Transactions are not consummated on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended), provided that Agility’s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended); CCXI Sponsor CCXI’s Sponsor, Churchill Sponsor XI LLC, is a Delaware limited liability company. MKA is the managing member of Sponsor. Michael Klein is the controlling shareholder of MKA and controls the management of Sponsor, including the exercise of voting and investment discretion over the securities of CCXI held by Sponsor. Sponsor is an affiliate of M. Klein and Company, LLC (“ M. Klein and Company ”), a global strategic advisory firm. M. Klein and Company provides CCXI with office space, administrative and support services pursuant to an administrative services agreement between the parties. Mr. Klein is the founder and managing partner of M. Klein and Company and acts as a strategic advisor to its clients. See section entitled “ Other Information Related to CCXI — Management, Directors and Executive Officers ” for biographical information on Mr. Klein. The general character of the Sponsor’s business is to provide capital to and to be the sponsor of CCXI. Sponsor’s roles and responsibilities included organizing, directing and managing the business and affairs of CCXI until the CCXI IPO. Currently, Sponsor assists CCXI in connection with identifying, investigating and completing an initial business combination. Background of the Transactions CCXI is a blank check company formed to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June 4, 2025. The business combination is the result of extensive work by CCXI, leveraging the Sponsor’s global network and the investing, operating and transaction experience of CCXI’s management team and members of the CCXI Board. The terms of the business combination are the result of arm’s -length negotiations between representatives of CCXI and representatives of Agility. The following is a brief discussion of the background of these negotiations, the Merger Agreement and the business combination. On December 16, 2025, CCXI completed its initial public offering. Prior to the consummation of the CCXI IPO, neither CCXI, nor anyone on its behalf, contacted any prospective target business or held any substantive discussions, formal or otherwise, with respect to a transaction with CCXI. After the CCXI IPO, CCXI commenced an active search for prospective businesses and assets to acquire. In evaluating potential businesses and assets to acquire, CCXI, together with the Sponsor and their advisors, surveyed the landscape of potential acquisition opportunities based on their knowledge of, and familiarity with, the M&A marketplace. In general, CCXI looked for acquisition targets that were of a size relevant to the public marketplace and positioned, operationally and financially, to be successful as a public company. CCXI further looked for those transactions that it believed, if entered, would be well received by the public markets. In particular, CCXI generally sought to identify companies that (i) generate or have the future potential to generate stable free cash -flow , (ii) would benefit uniquely from CCXI’s capabilities, (iii) are sourced through CCXI’s proprietary channels, (iv) have a committed and capable management team and (v) have the potential to grow through both organic growth and acquisition opportunities. CCXI also sought to identify companies that it believed would benefit from being a publicly -held entity, particularly with respect to access to capital for both organic growth and for use in acquisitions, with a particular emphasis on opportunities that are primed to unlock disruptive technological advancements. CCXI generally implements these criteria when evaluating potential targets. Central to CCXI’s strategy was to originate an investment opportunity sourced through its proprietary channels. CCXI’s selection process leveraged the Sponsor’s network of industry, venture capital sponsor and private equity sponsor relationships as well as relationships with management teams of public and private companies, investment bankers, attorneys and accountants. Starting in December 2025 and continuing through early 2026, following the closing of the CCXI IPO, representatives of Archimedes Advisor Group LLC, CCXI’s strategic advisor and affiliate of Michael Klein, Chairman of the Board of CCXI (“ Archimedes ”), at the direction of CCXI, and the Sponsor commenced a search for prospective business combination candidates (“ targets ”) for CCXI to partner with in its initial business combination. CCXI, with the assistance of Archimedes, developed a list of approximately a dozen targets leveraging the proprietary sourcing channels described above. Representatives of CCXI were also contacted by potential targets that they had not previously identified through its search process. In certain instances, it was requested by a potential target that CCXI enter into a non -disclosure agreement. CCXI did so on a selective basis, entering into fewer than ten such agreements. Prior to entering into a non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI did not submit a non -binding letter of intent to any prospective target other than Agility. Upon entering into the non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI became subject to an exclusivity provision that precluded CCXI from participating in discussions or negotiations with any other potential target regarding a prospective business combination. 119 Table of Contents On January 7, 2026, Mr. Klein held a videoconference call with Agility’s Chief Executive Officer, Ms. Margaret “Peggy” Johnson. Mr. Klein and Ms. Johnson have a long -standing professional relationship, including from Mr. Klein’s service on the board of Magic Leap during Ms. Johnson’s tenure as its Chief Executive Officer. The call was scheduled for Ms. Johnson to provide an update on Agility, particularly following its recent attendance at the Consumer Electronics Show (widely referred to as “CES”). Ms. Johnson shared that Agility was experiencing strong momentum in its business and was interested in evaluating potential options to become the first publicly traded pure -play humanoid robotics company. On March 2, 2026, CCXI sent an initial non -binding LOI to Agility’s advisor, BTIG. The initial proposal contemplated a business combination between CCXI and Agility whereby Agility would combine with CCXI in a transaction ascribing a pre -money equity value for Agility of $2,500 - $3,000 million, together with detailed further transaction terms. In establishing the pre -money equity value range set forth above, CCXI considered the approximately $2,000 million post -money equity value ascribed to Agility in its Series C3 financing round. CCXI indicated to Agility that the preliminary pre -money equity value was subject to additional due diligence and that CCXI would require a fairness opinion from an independent third -party valuation firm before entering into a transaction with Agility. Prior to submission of the LOI, CCXI and Agility had not previously discussed the pre -money equity value range 120 Table of Contents proposed by CCXI. CCXI and Agility did not agree on a precise equity value until, as further described below, the parties agreed to a $2,500 million equity value in connection with engaging prospective PIPE Investors beginning on May 7, 2026. The initial letter of intent from CCXI provided that the consideration to be paid in the business combination with Agility would consist entirely of newly issued shares of the Post -Closing Company’s common stock valued at the price per share of funds held in the trust account as of the Closing. The proposal further contemplated a post -Closing lock -up for the Sponsor and Agility’s shareholders, restricting the transfer of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock to be received in the business combination, with 100% of the share consideration being locked up for 180 days post -Closing , subject to early release based on stock price performance. Included in the proposal letter was a mutual 45 -day exclusivity period to allow CCXI to complete its due diligence and to allow the parties to negotiate and finalize definitive documentation. The initial proposal also contemplated that prior to the execution of the business combination, the parties would work together to obtain binding written commitments from institutional investors for an aggregate of $200 million in gross proceeds in a private placement of equity securities of the surviving Post -Closing Company (the “PIPE”). The LOI included a request by CCXI that Agility secure from its existing equityholders participation in the PIPE. From March 2, 2026 through March 15, 2026, Agility, with the assistance of its advisors, Latham & Watkins LLP (“ Latham ”) and BTIG’s M&A advisory team, negotiated the non -binding LOI with CCXI. On March 13, 2026, Agility responded to CCXI’s initial proposal, accepting the pre -money equity valuation range, lock -up terms, and target PIPE size of $200 million. Agility revised the PIPE provisions to provide that it would use reasonable best efforts to obtain participation from its existing equityholders and also introduced a minimum cash condition, without specifying a minimum cash amount. On March 15, 2026, CCXI sent a revised proposal to Agility that accepted Agility’s proposed revisions to the PIPE provisions, while providing for a target of at least $50 million of participation from Agility’s existing equityholders. CCXI also accepted the concept of a minimum cash condition and proposed a threshold of $200 million, consisting of the funds remaining in CCXI’s Trust Account after giving effect to all pre -Closing redemptions, but before payment of any Transaction Expenses or unpaid Sponsor loans, plus the proceeds from the PIPE or any Company Bridge Financing. CCXI also proposed revisions to select certain other non -material provisions of the LOI. Reasons for Approval of the Transactions The CCXI Board, in evaluating the Transactions, consulted with CCXI’s management and financial, technical and legal advisors. In (1) resolving that it is fair to and in the best interests of CCXI and its shareholders, and declaring it advisable, to enter into the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions, (2) approving the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions, including the Merger, on the terms and subject to the conditions of the Merger Agreement, and (3) adopting a resolution recommending the business combination proposal be approved by CCXI shareholders, the CCXI Board considered and evaluated a number of factors, including the factors discussed below. The CCXI Board did not consider it practicable to, and did not attempt to, quantify or otherwise assign relative weights to the specific factors it considered in reaching its determination. In addition, individual directors may have given different weight to different factors. The CCXI Board viewed its decision as being based on all of the information available and the factors presented to and considered by it. This explanation of CCXI’s reasons for the Transactions and all other information presented in this section is forward -looking in nature and, therefore, should be read in light of the factors discussed in the section entitled “ Cautionary Note Regarding Forward -Looking Statements .” 125 Table of Contents The CCXI Board considered a number of factors pertaining to the Transactions as generally supporting its decision to enter into the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party, and the Transactions, including but not limited to, the following material factors: • Reasonableness of Aggregate Consideration .    Following a review of the financial data provided to CCXI, including Agility’s historical financial statements and certain unaudited prospective financial information, CCXI’s due diligence review of Agility’s business and the views of CCXI’s financial advisor (which supported CCXI management’s view regarding valuation), the CCXI Board considered the aggregate consideration to be paid and determined that the aggregate consideration was reasonable in light of such data and financial information. • Business and Financial Condition and Prospects .    After conducting extensive due diligence, the CCXI Board and CCXI’s management team obtained a better understanding of Agility’s business, financial condition, management team and future growth prospects. The CCXI Board considered the results of the due diligence review of Agility’s business, as further described in “— Background of the Transactions, ” as well as Agility’s management team’s experience. The CCXI Board considered how these factors will enhance Agility’s ability to scale effectively and to execute upon and achieve its business plan. • Financings and Minimum Cash Condition. The CCXI Board considered the fact that Agility would need additional financing to pursue its business plan in setting the Minimum Cash Condition, and in that regard considered Agility’s active pursuit of additional equity financing opportunities and strategic transactions, including Agility SAFEs and the potential to raise a PIPE Investment, together which were expected to be sufficient to satisfy the Minimum Cash Condition, as further described in “— Background of the Transactions.” • Experienced and Committed Management Team .    The CCXI Board considered that the Post -Closing Company is expected to continue to be led by Agility’s senior management team, whose collective experience includes the development of humanoid robotics and physical AI technologies, the commercialization of enterprise technology products, and the scaling of technology businesses. The CCXI Board also considered that the senior management team has led Agility’s evolution from technology development to commercial deployment with leading customers and is expected to remain with the Post -Closing Company in the capacity of officers and/or directors, providing continuity in executing the Post -Closing Company’s business strategy. • Opinion of CCXI’s Financial Advisor .    The CCXI Board took into account the financial presentation, orally presented to the CCXI Board on June 22, 2026, and the written opinion, dated as of June 23, 2026, of Ocean Tomo to the CCXI Board as to the fairness, from a financial point of view and as of the date of the opinion, of the Purchase Price to CCXI’s shareholders (other than the Sponsor), which opinion was based on and subject to the matters considered, the procedures followed, the assumptions made and various limitations of and qualifications to the review undertaken as more fully described under the section entitled “ — Opinion of CCXI’s Financial Advisor ” below. • Commitment of Agility’s Owners .    The CCXI Board considered the fact that Agility’s Chief Executive Officer and other key executives, together with all of the other shareholders of Agility, are not selling any of their current shareholdings of Agility in the Transaction, which the CCXI Board believed reflects such shareholders’ belief in and commitment to the continued growth prospects of Agility going forward. • Other Alternatives .    CCXI raised $414,000,000 in 2025 with the objective of consummating an attractive business combination. Since that time, as more fully described in “ — Background of the Transactions ,” CCXI has evaluated a number of businesses but has been most impressed by the Agility business. The CCXI Board believed that, based upon the terms of the Transactions, the Transactions provide the best available opportunity to maximize value for CCXI shareholders. • Terms of the Merger Agreement and the Related Agreements .    The CCXI Board considered the terms and conditions of the Merger Agreement and the related agreements and the transactions contemplated thereby, including the Merger, each party’s representations, warranties and covenants, the conditions to each party’s obligation to consummate the transactions contemplated thereby and the termination provisions, as well as the strong commitment by both Agility and CCXI to complete the Transactions. 126 Table of Contents • Board of Directors of the Post -Closing Company .    The CCXI Board considered that the initial Post -Closing Company Board would be comprised of seven or nine directors, who shall include (1) one director designated by Sponsor (to be designated as a Class III director), in the case of a seven -director board, or two directors designated by Sponsor (one of which to be designated as a Class I director and one of which to be designated as a Class III director), in the case of a nine -director board, and (2) such other individuals determined by Agility, in its sole and exclusive discretion, provided that the citizenship of the members of the Post -Closing Company Board shall be such that CCXI will be free of foreign ownership, control or domination. The CCXI Board also considered a variety of uncertainties and risks and other potentially negative factors concerning the Transactions, including, but not limited to, the following: • Macroeconomic Risks .    Macroeconomic uncertainty and the effects it could have on the combined company’s revenues. • Benefits May Not Be Achieved .    The risk that the potential benefits of the Transactions may not be fully achieved or may not be achieved within the expected timeframe. • Technology Development Risks. The risk that Agility may not continue to successfully develop, manufacture and deploy commercially viable humanoid robotics and physical AI technologies or achieve anticipated technological advancements necessary to support its long -term business strategy. • Customer Adoption Risks. Large -scale commercialization of Agility’s humanoid robotics technology, including broad customer adoption of Digit across warehouse, manufacturing and other industrial applications, may be delayed or develop more slowly than expected, and Agility may not successfully expand existing customer relationships or convert pilot programs and customer interest into long -term commercial deployments. • Manufacturing and Cost Reduction Risks. The risk that Agility may not successfully scale manufacturing operations, manage its supply chain, reduce the bill of materials and production costs for Digit, or achieve anticipated manufacturing efficiencies and production volumes necessary to support its long -term financial performance. • Regulatory Risks. The risk that laws, regulations and industry standards applicable to humanoid robots operating in workplace environments, including standards relating to safety and human -robot interaction, may evolve in ways that delay or limit the commercial deployment or adoption of Agility’s products or require modifications to its products or operations. • Competitive Risks. The risk that existing or new competitors may develop competing humanoid robotics or physical AI technologies or products that achieve greater commercial acceptance, technological advantages or more rapid market adoption than Agility’s products. • Liquidation .    The risks and costs to CCXI if the business combination is not completed, including the risk of diverting management focus and resources from other business combination opportunities, which could result in CCXI being unable to effect a business combination within the completion window and force CCXI to liquidate. • Shareholder Vote .    The risk that CCXI’s shareholders may object to and challenge the Transactions and take action that may prevent or delay the consummation of the Transactions, including to vote down the proposals at the extraordinary general meeting or redeem their shares. • Closing Conditions .    The fact that completion of the Transactions is conditioned on the satisfaction of certain closing conditions that are not within CCXI’s control. • CCXI Public Shareholders Holding a Minority Position in the Post -Combination Company .    The risk that CCXI public shareholders will hold a minority position in the post -combination company (approximately          %, assuming that no shares of CCXI common stock are elected to be redeemed by CCXI shareholders), which may reduce the influence that CCXI’s current shareholders have on the management of CCXI. 127 Table of Contents • Litigation .    The possibility of litigation challenging the Transactions or that an adverse judgment granting injunctive relief could enjoin or otherwise interfere with the consummation of the Transactions. • Fees and Expenses .    The fees and expenses associated with completing the Transactions. • Other Risks .    Various other risks associated with the business of Agility, as described in the section entitled “ Risk Factors ” appearing elsewhere in this proxy statement. In addition to considering the factors described above, the CCXI Board also considered that: • Interests of Certain Persons .    Some officers and directors of CCXI have interests in the Transactions as individuals that are in addition to, and that may be different from, the interests of CCXI shareholders (see section entitled “— Interests of Certain CCXI Persons in the Business Combination ”). CCXI’s independent directors reviewed and considered these interests during the negotiation of the business combination and in evaluating and unanimously approving, as members of the CCXI Board, the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions. The independent directors of CCXI did not retain an unaffiliated representative to act solely on behalf of unaffiliated security holders for purposes of negotiating the terms of the Merger Agreement and/or preparing a report concerning the approval of the Merger Agreement. The CCXI Board concluded that the potential benefits that it expected CCXI and its shareholders to achieve as a result of the Transactions outweighed the potentially negative factors associated with the Transactions. The CCXI Board also noted that CCXI shareholders would have a substantial economic interest in the combined company (depending on the level of CCXI shareholders that sought redemption of their CCXI public shares into cash). Accordingly, the CCXI Board unanimously determined that the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions are fair to, and in the best interests of, CCXI and its shareholders. Agility’s Reasons for Engaging in the Transactions In evaluating the Transactions, the Agility board considered a number of factors pertaining to the Transactions, including the following principle purposes: • Access to Public Capital Markets .    Agility is an early -stage technology company that has funded its operations to date through private capital raises. The Agility Board considered that becoming a publicly traded company on a major U.S. stock exchange through the business combination would provide Agility with access to the U.S. public capital markets, enabling Agility to raise additional capital to support the commercialization and large -scale manufacturing of Digit, scale operations, execute its long -term growth strategy and provide Agility with greater financial flexibility and a broader range of capital -raising alternatives than are typically available to a privately held company. • Immediate Capital Infusion The Transactions, together with the PIPE Investment of up to $201,025,000, and the potential availability of cash from the CCXI trust account, are expected to provide Agility with a substantial capital infusion at the Closing to support its commercialization, manufacturing scale -up and operating needs. The Agility Board considered this an important advantage over other paths to public listing that may not provide a concurrent capital raise of comparable certainty and magnitude. • Enhanced Visibility and Brand Awareness .    Becoming a publicly traded company would enhance Agility’s visibility and brand recognition in the market, which may support commercial adoption of Agility’s humanoid robotics and physical AI solutions, strengthen customer confidence, and facilitate strategic partnerships with leading companies. • Talent Attraction and Retention. The Agility Board considered that the business combination would enhance Agility’s ability to attract, incentivize and retain high -quality talent by enabling the company to offer employees and prospective hires equity -based compensation in the form of publicly traded securities, which the Agility Board believes would increase the attractiveness and perceived value of such awards and strengthen Agility’s ability to compete for talent in a highly competitive market. • Ability to Use Equity as Currency .    As a public company, Agility would have the ability to use its publicly traded common stock as consideration for potential future acquisitions and strategic investments, which the Agility Board believes would enhance Agility’s flexibility in pursuing strategic transactions and support its long -term growth objectives. 128 Table of Contents Benefits and Detriments of the Business Combination and Related Financing Transactions Benefits and Detriments of the Business Combination Stakeholder Benefits Detriments CCXI The completion of the business combination avoids the liquidation of the trust account and is expected to create value for CCXI and its shareholders. The Unit Economics should not be viewed as a projection or forecast of Agility’s overall financial performance. Furthermore, the Unit Economics do not take into account any circumstances or events occurring after the date on which such Unit Economics were prepared, which was April 20, 2026, and may differ, perhaps significantly, from similarly titled measures that may be presented in the future. As such, the Unit Economics do not reflect any updates since the time such Unit Economics were delivered to the CCXI Board and Ocean Tomo on April 20, 2026. Moreover, the Unit Economics are not subject to any escalation or discounting. The time at which the assumptions underlying the Unit Economics will be realized, if at all, is highly uncertain. As a result, there can be no assurance that the Unit Economics will be realized or that actual performance will yield similar results (i.e., not significantly higher or lower than those set forth in the Unit Economics). Because the Unit Economics relate to estimates at scale, the timing of which is uncertain, such information by its nature becomes less predictive with the passage of time. The definitions of the non -GAAP measures included in the Unit Economics may not align with those underlying the non -GAAP measures presented in the section entitled “ Agility’s Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations. ” Further, other companies, including companies in our industry, may calculate these metrics differently or not at all, which reduces their usefulness as comparative measures.
