Introduction CCXI is a blank check company formed in order to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June 4, 2025. CCXI’s efforts to identify a prospective target business were not limited to any particular industry or geographic region. Prior to executing the Merger Agreement, CCXI’s efforts were limited to organizational activities, completion of the CCXI IPO and the evaluation of initial business combination candidates. Initial Public Offering and Simultaneous Private Placement On December 18, 2025, CCXI consummated its initial public offering of 41,400,000 CCXI public units, including 5,400,000 CCXI public units under the underwriters’ over -allotment option. The CCXI public units were sold at an offering price of $10.00 per unit, generating gross proceeds to CCXI of $414,000,000. Simultaneously with the consummation of the CCXI IPO and the exercise of the underwriters’ over -allotment option, CCXI consummated the private placement of 500,000 private placement units to the Sponsor at a purchase price of $10.00 per unit, generating gross proceeds of $5,000,000. Transaction costs amounted to $19,618,232, consisting of $3,000,000 of underwriting fees, $15,990,000 of deferred underwriting fees (of which $1,500,000 has been paid and $14,490,000 remains deferred) and $628,232 of other offering costs. Following the consummation of the CCXI IPO, $414,000,000 was deposited into a U.S. -based trust account (the “ trust account ”) with Continental Stock Transfer & Trust Company acting as trustee (the “ trustee ”). Except as described in the prospectus for the CCXI IPO, these proceeds will not be released until the earlier of the completion of an initial business combination and CCXI’s redemption of 100% of the outstanding CCXI public shares upon its failure to consummate an initial business combination within the completion window. Working Capital Loans In addition, in order to finance transaction costs in connection with its initial business combination, the Sponsor or an affiliate of the Sponsor, or the CCXI’s officers and directors may, but are not obligated to, loan CCXI funds as may be required (“ Working Capital Loans ”). If CCXI completes its initial business combination, CCXI would repay the Working Capital Loans. In the event that the initial business combination does not close, CCXI may use a portion of proceeds held outside the trust account to repay the Working Capital Loans but no proceeds held in the trust account would be used to repay the Working Capital Loans. If the Sponsor makes any Working Capital Loans, up to $3,000,000 of such loans may be convertible into units of the Post -Closing Company at a price of $10.00 per unit at the option of the lender. The units and their underlying securities would be identical to the CCXI private placement units. As of June 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, CCXI had no borrowings under such loans. On July 2, 2026, we issued an unsecured promissory note in the aggregate principal amount of up to $1,500,000 to the Sponsor (the “ July 2026 Note ”), for working capital needs. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, we have borrowed the full $1,500,000 available under the July 2026 Note. On August 7, 2026, CCXI issued an additional unsecured promissory note in the aggregate principal amount of up to $1,500,000 (the “ August 2026 Note ”), for working capital needs. The August 2026 Note may be convertible into units of the Post -Closing Company at a price of $10.00 per unit at the option of the lender. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, CCXI has borrowed $750,000 under the August 2026 Note. Both the July 2026 Note and the August 2026 Note mature upon the earlier of the closing of CCXI’s initial business combination or CCXI’s liquidation. Conflicts of Interest As a matter of Cayman Islands law, a director owes three types of duties to the company: (i) statutory duties, (ii) fiduciary duties, and (iii) common law duties. The Cayman Companies Act imposes a number of statutory duties on a director. A Cayman Islands director’s fiduciary duties are not codified, however, the courts of the Cayman Islands have held that a director owes the following fiduciary duties (a) a duty to act in what the director bona fide considers to be in the best interests of the company, (b) a duty to exercise their powers for the purposes they were conferred, (c) a duty to avoid fettering his or her discretion in the future and (d) a duty to avoid conflicts of interest and of duty. The common law duties owed by a director are those to act with skill, care and diligence that may reasonably be expected of a person carrying out the same functions as are carried out by that director in relation to the company and, also, to act with the skill, care and diligence in keeping with a standard of care commensurate with any particular skill they have which enables them to meet a higher standard than a director without those skills. In fulfilling their duty of care to us, our directors must ensure compliance with the CCXI current articles of association, as amended and restated from time to time. As set out above, directors have a duty not to put themselves in a position of conflict. However, in some instances what would otherwise be a breach of this duty can be forgiven and/or authorized in advance by the shareholders provided that there is full disclosure by the directors. This can be done by way of permission granted in the CCXI current articles of association or alternatively by shareholder approval at shareholder meetings. Our management team is responsible for the management of our affairs. As described above and below, each of our officers and directors presently has, and any of them in the future may have additional, fiduciary or contractual obligations to another entity pursuant to which such officer or director is or will be required to present a business combination opportunity to such entity. Accordingly, if any of our officers or directors becomes aware of a business combination opportunity which is suitable for an entity to which he or she has then current fiduciary or contractual obligations, he or she will honor his or her fiduciary or contractual obligations to present such business combination opportunity to such other entity, subject to their fiduciary duties under Cayman Islands law. The CCXI current articles of association provide that, to the fullest extent permitted by law: (1) no individual serving as a director or an officer, among other persons, shall have any duty, except and to the extent expressly assumed by contract, to refrain from engaging directly or indirectly in the same or similar business activities or lines of business as us, and (2) we renounce any interest or expectancy in, or in being offered an opportunity to participate in, any potential transaction or matter which (a) may be a corporate opportunity for any director or officer, on the one hand, and us, on the other or (b) the presentation of which would breach an existing legal obligation of a director or officer to any other entity. We do not believe, however, that the fiduciary duties or contractual obligations of our officers or directors will materially affect our ability to complete our initial business combination. In addition, our Sponsor, officers, directors, and strategic and operating partners may participate in the formation of, or become an officer or director of, any other blank check company prior to completion of our initial business combination. As a result, our sponsor, officers, directors, the Sponsor and our affiliates could have conflicts of interest 203 Table of Contents in determining whether to present business combination opportunities to us or to any other blank check company with which they may become involved. The Sponsor, Mr. Klein and our strategic and operating partners have complete discretion, subject to applicable fiduciary duties, as to which blank check company they choose to pursue a business combination and the order in which they pursue business combinations for any of their existing or future blank check companies. As a result, the Sponsor, Mr. Klein and our strategic and operating partners may pursue business combinations for blank check companies that they have sponsored in any order, which could result in its more recent blank check companies completing business combinations prior to their blank check companies that were launched earlier. There are no contractual obligations governing the allocation of opportunities among the various blank check companies. Any determination as to which blank check company will pursue a particular acquisition target will be made based on the circumstances of the particular situation, including, but not limited to, the relative sizes of the blank check companies compared to the sizes of the targets, the need or desire for additional financings and the relevant experience of the directors, officers and our partners involved with a particular blank check company. Below is a table summarizing the entities to which our officers and directors currently have fiduciary duties, contractual obligations or other material management relationships. The fiduciary duties owed by such individuals are prescribed by applicable law based on the jurisdiction of such entity’s incorporation, formation or organization. We do not believe, however, that the fiduciary, contractual or other obligations or duties of our officers or directors, or of the Sponsor and our affiliates, or policies applicable to the Sponsor or any of our partners, will materially affect our ability to complete our initial business combination. Potential investors should also be aware of the following other potential conflicts of interest: • None of our officers or directors is required to commit his or her full time to our affairs and, accordingly, may have conflicts of interest in allocating his or her time among various business activities. • In the course of their other business activities, our officers and directors may become aware of investment and business opportunities which may be appropriate for presentation to us as well as the other entities with which they are affiliated. Our management may have conflicts of interest in determining to which entity a particular business opportunity should be presented. Please see “— Management, Directors and Executive Officers ” for a description of our management’s other affiliations. • Our Sponsor, officers and directors have agreed to waive their redemption rights with respect to any founder shares, private placement shares and any public shares held by them in connection with the consummation of our initial business combination. Additionally, our initial shareholders, officers and directors have agreed to waive their rights to liquidating distributions from the trust account with respect to any founder shares or private placement shares held by them if we fail to consummate our initial business combination within the completion window. However, if our initial shareholders or any of our officers, directors or affiliates acquire public shares, they will be entitled to liquidating distributions from the trust account with respect to such public shares if we fail to consummate our initial business combination within the completion window. If we do not complete our initial business combination within such applicable time period, the proceeds of the sale of the private placement units held in the trust account will be used to fund the redemption of our public shares, and the private placement warrants will expire worthless. With certain limited exceptions, the founder shares will not be transferable, assignable or salable by our initial shareholders until the earlier of: (1) six months following the consummation of our initial business combination; or (2) subsequent to the consummation of our initial business combination, the date on which we consummate a transaction which results in all of our shareholders having the right to exchange their shares for cash, securities, or other property subject to certain limited exceptions. With certain limited exceptions, the private placement warrants and the ordinary shares underlying such warrants, will not be transferable, assignable or salable by our sponsor until 30 days after the completion of our initial business combination. Since our sponsor, officers and directors will directly or indirectly own ordinary shares and warrants following this offering, our officers and directors may have a conflict of interest in determining whether a particular target business is an appropriate business with which to effectuate our initial business combination. • Our key personnel may negotiate employment or consulting agreements with a target business in connection with a particular business combination. These agreements may provide for them to receive compensation following our initial business combination and as a result, may cause them to have conflicts of interest in determining whether to proceed with a particular business combination. 204 Table of Contents • Our key personnel may have a conflict of interest with respect to evaluating a particular business combination if the retention or resignation of any such key personnel was included by a target business as a condition to any agreement with respect to our initial business combination. Fair Market Value of Target Business The target business or businesses that CCXI acquires must collectively have a fair market value equal to at least 80% of the balance of the funds in the trust account (net of amounts withdrawn to fund certain working capital requirements and/or to pay our taxes and excluding the deferred underwriting fees from the CCXI IPO held in the trust account) at the time of the execution of a definitive agreement for an initial business combination, although CCXI 205 Table of Contents may acquire a target business whose fair market value significantly exceeds 80% of the trust account balance. The CCXI Board determined that this test was met in connection with the business combination, as described in the section entitled “ Proposal No. 1 — The Business Combination Proposal — Satisfaction of the 80% Test .” Shareholder Approval of an Initial Business Combination Under the CCXI current articles of association, in connection with any proposed initial business combination, CCXI must seek shareholder approval of such initial business combination at a meeting called for such purpose in connection with which CCXI public shareholders may seek to redeem their CCXI public shares for cash, regardless of whether they vote “for” or “against” the proposed initial business combination, subject to the limitations described in the prospectus for the CCXI IPO. Accordingly, in connection with the business combination, CCXI public shareholders may seek to redeem their CCXI public shares for cash in accordance with the procedures set forth in this proxy statement/prospectus. Voting Restrictions in Connection with Shareholder Meeting Pursuant to the terms of the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have each agreed to vote their CCXI Ordinary Shares, including any CCXI Founder Shares and CCXI private placement shares held by them as of the CCXI record date, in favor of the business combination proposal and the other proposals described in this proxy statement/prospectus. At any time prior to the extraordinary general meeting, during a period when they are not then aware of any material nonpublic information regarding CCXI or its securities, the Sponsor, Agility and/or their respective affiliates may purchase shares from institutional and other investors that vote, or indicate an intention to vote, against the business combination proposal, or execute agreements to purchase such shares from them in the future, or they may enter into transactions with such persons and others to provide them with incentives to acquire CCXI Ordinary Shares, not redeem their CCXI Ordinary Shares in connection with the business combination or vote their shares in favor of the business combination proposal. The purpose of such share purchases and other transactions would be to increase the likelihood of satisfaction of the requirements for the business combination to be approved if it appears that such requirements would otherwise not be met. Redemption of CCXI Public Shares and Liquidation if No Initial Business Combination If CCXI is unable to complete the business combination within the completion window and CCXI does not hold a shareholder vote to amend the CCXI current articles of association to extend the amount of time it has to consummate a business combination, CCXI will: (1) cease all operations except for the purpose of winding up; (2) as promptly as reasonably possible but not more than ten business days thereafter (and subject to lawfully available funds therefor), redeem the CCXI public shares, at a per share price, payable in cash, equal to the aggregate amount then on deposit in the trust account including interest earned on the funds held in the trust account (which interest shall be net of permitted withdrawals and less up to $100,000 of interest to pay dissolution expenses and net of taxes payable), divided by the number of then outstanding CCXI public shares, which redemption will completely extinguish CCXI public shareholders’ rights as shareholders (including the right to receive further liquidating distributions, if any), subject to applicable law; and (3) as promptly as reasonably possible following such redemption, subject to the approval of remaining shareholders and the CCXI Board, liquidate and dissolve, subject in each case to CCXI’s obligations under Cayman Islands law to provide for claims of creditors and the requirements of other applicable law. There will be no redemption rights or liquidating distributions with respect to CCXI Warrants, which will expire without value to the holder if CCXI fails to complete the initial business combination within the completion window. Our Sponsor, officers and directors will not be entitled to rights to liquidating distributions from the trust account with respect to any CCXI Founder Shares or CCXI private placement shares held by them if CCXI fails to complete the initial business combination within the completion window. However, if the Sponsor, officers or directors acquire CCXI public shares in or after the CCXI IPO, they will be entitled to liquidating distributions from the trust account with respect to such CCXI public shares if CCXI fails to complete the initial business combination within the completion window. Our Sponsor, officers and directors have agreed that they will not propose any amendment to the CCXI current articles of association (1) in a manner that would affect the substance or timing of CCXI’s obligation to redeem 100% of the CCXI public shares if CCXI does not complete an initial business combination within the completion window or (2) with 206 Table of Contents respect to any other provision relating to the right of holders of the CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares or pre -initial business combination activity, unless CCXI provides the CCXI public shareholders with the opportunity to redeem their CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares upon approval of any such amendment at a per share price, payable in cash, equal to the aggregate amount then on deposit in the trust account, including interest earned on the funds held in the trust account (which interest shall be net of permitted withdrawals), divided by the number of then outstanding CCXI public shares. Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, such an amendment would need to be approved by a special resolution. We expect that all costs and expenses associated with implementing CCXI’s liquidation, as well as payments to any creditors, will be funded from amounts remaining out of the proceeds held outside the trust account, although CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that there will be sufficient funds for such purpose. However, if those funds are not sufficient to cover the costs and expenses associated with implementing CCXI’s liquidation, to the extent that there is any interest accrued in the trust account following permitted withdrawals, CCXI may request the trustee to release to CCXI an additional amount of up to $100,000 of such accrued interest to pay those costs and expenses. If CCXI were to expend all of the net proceeds of the CCXI IPO and the sale of the CCXI private placement units, other than the proceeds deposited in the trust account, and without taking into account interest, if any, earned on the trust account, the per share redemption amount received by shareholders upon CCXI’s dissolution would be approximately $10.00. The proceeds deposited in the trust account could, however, become subject to the claims of CCXI’s creditors which would have higher priority than the claims of the CCXI public shareholders. CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that the actual per share redemption amount received by shareholders will not be substantially less than $10.00. While CCXI intends to pay such amounts, if any, CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that CCXI will have funds sufficient to pay or provide for all creditors’ claims. Although CCXI will seek to have all vendors, service providers (other than CCXI’s independent registered public accounting firm), prospective target businesses and other entities with which CCXI does business execute agreements with CCXI waiving any right, title, interest or claim of any kind in or to any monies held in the trust account for the benefit of the CCXI public shareholders, there is no guarantee that they will execute such agreements or even if they execute such agreements that they would be prevented from bringing claims against the trust account including but not limited to fraudulent inducement, breach of fiduciary responsibility or other similar claims, as well as claims challenging the enforceability of the waiver, in each case in order to gain an advantage with respect to a claim against CCXI’s assets, including the funds held in the trust account. If any third party refuses to execute an agreement waiving such claims to the monies held in the trust account, CCXI’s management will perform an analysis of the alternatives available to it and will only enter into an agreement with a third party that has not executed a waiver if management believes that such third party’s engagement would be significantly more beneficial to CCXI than any alternative. Examples of possible instances where CCXI may engage a third party that refuses to execute a waiver include the engagement of a third party consultant whose particular expertise or skills are believed by management to be significantly superior to those of other consultants that would agree to execute a waiver or in cases where CCXI is unable to find a service provider willing to execute a waiver. In addition, there is no guarantee that such entities will agree to waive any claims they may have in the future as a result of, or arising out of, any negotiations, contracts or agreements with CCXI and will not seek recourse against the trust account for any reason. Our Sponsor has agreed that it will be liable to CCXI if and to the extent any claims by a third party (other than CCXI’s independent public accounting firm) for services rendered or products sold to us, or a prospective target business with which CCXI has entered into a written letter of intent, confidentiality or other similar agreement or business combination agreement, reduce the amount of funds in the trust account to below (1) $10.00 per CCXI public share or (2) such lesser amount per CCXI public share held in the trust account as of the date of the liquidation of the trust account, due to reductions in value of the trust assets, in each case net of permitted withdrawals, except as to any claims by a third party that executed a waiver of any and all rights to the monies held in the trust account (whether or not such waiver is enforceable) and except as to any claims under CCXI’s indemnity of the underwriters of the CCXI IPO against certain liabilities, including liabilities under the Securities Act. However, CCXI has not asked the Sponsor to reserve for such indemnification obligations, nor has CCXI independently verified whether the Sponsor has sufficient funds to satisfy its indemnity obligations, and CCXI believes that the Sponsor’s only assets are securities of the Company. Therefore, CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that the Sponsor would be able to satisfy those obligations. As a result, if any such claims were successfully made against the trust account, the funds available for the initial business combination and redemptions could be reduced to less than $10.00 per CCXI public share. In such event, CCXI may not be able to complete the initial business combination, and CCXI’s shareholders would receive such lesser amount per share in connection with any redemption of their CCXI public shares. None of CCXI’s officers or directors will indemnify CCXI for claims by third parties including, without limitation, claims by vendors and prospective target businesses. 207 Table of Contents In the event that the proceeds in the trust account are reduced below (1) $10.00 per CCXI public share or (2) such lesser amount per CCXI public share held in the trust account as of the date of the liquidation of the trust account, due to reductions in value of the trust assets, in each case net of permitted withdrawals, and the Sponsor asserts that it is unable to satisfy its indemnification obligations or that it has no indemnification obligations related to a particular claim, CCXI’s independent directors would determine whether to take legal action against the Sponsor to enforce its indemnification obligations. While CCXI currently expects that CCXI’s independent directors would take legal action on CCXI’s behalf against the Sponsor to enforce its indemnification obligations to us, it is possible that CCXI’s independent directors in exercising their business judgment may choose not to do so if, for example, the cost of such legal action is deemed by the independent directors to be too high relative to the amount recoverable or if the independent directors determine that a favorable outcome is not likely. CCXI has not asked the Sponsor to reserve for such indemnification obligations and CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that the Sponsor would be able to satisfy those obligations. Accordingly, CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that due to claims of creditors the actual value of the per share redemption price will not be less than $10.00 per CCXI public share. CCXI will seek to reduce the possibility that the Sponsor will have to indemnify the trust account due to claims of creditors by endeavoring to have all vendors, service providers (other than CCXI’s independent registered public accounting firm), prospective target businesses or other entities with which CCXI does business execute agreements with CCXI waiving any right, title, interest or claim of any kind in or to monies held in the trust account. CCXI had access to proceeds of the CCXI IPO and CCXI Private Placement, as well as permitted withdrawals, with which to pay any such potential claims (including costs and expenses incurred in connection with CCXI’s liquidation, currently estimated to be no more than approximately $100,000). In the event that CCXI liquidates and it is subsequently determined that the reserve for claims and liabilities is insufficient, shareholders who received funds from the trust account could be liable for claims made by creditors. If CCXI files a winding up petition or a winding up petition is filed against CCXI that is not dismissed, the proceeds held in the trust account could be subject to applicable bankruptcy or insolvency law, and a liquidator may determine that such funds should be included in CCXI’s bankruptcy or insolvency estate and subject to the claims of third -party creditors with priority over the claims of CCXI’s shareholders. To the extent any bankruptcy or insolvency claims deplete the trust account, CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that CCXI will be able to return $10.00 per share to the CCXI public shareholders. Additionally, if CCXI files a winding up petition or a winding up petition is filed against CCXI that is not dismissed, any distributions received by shareholders could be subject to challenge under applicable debtor/creditor and/or insolvency laws as a “voidable preference” or a “fraudulent conveyance, preference or disposition.” As a result, a liquidator or a bankruptcy or other court could seek to recover some or all amounts received by CCXI’s shareholders. Furthermore, the CCXI Board may be viewed as having breached its fiduciary duty to CCXI or CCXI’s creditors and/or may have acted in bad faith, and thereby exposing itself and the Company to claims of punitive damages, by paying CCXI public shareholders from the trust account prior to addressing the claims of creditors. CCXI cannot assure CCXI’s shareholders that claims will not be brought against CCXI for these reasons. Director Independence The rules of Nasdaq require that a majority of the CCXI Board generally must be independent, subject to certain limited exceptions set forth thereunder. An “independent director” is defined generally as a person other than an officer or employee of the company or its subsidiaries or any other individual having a relationship which, in the opinion of the company’s board of directors, would interfere with the director’s exercise of independent judgment in carrying out the responsibilities of a director. The CCXI Board has determined that each of Mr. Murphy, Mr. Sherman and Mr. Lapping is an independent director under applicable SEC and Nasdaq Rules. Our independent directors have regularly scheduled meetings at which only independent directors are present. Number and Terms of Office of Officers and Directors The CCXI Board consists of four members. The CCXI Board is divided into three classes with only one class of directors being elected in each year and each class (except for those directors appointed prior to our first annual meeting of shareholders) serving a three -year term. The term of office of the first class of directors, consisting of Mr. Sherman, will expire at our first annual general meeting. The term of office of the second class of directors, consisting of Mr. Murphy, will expire at the second annual general meeting. The term of office of the third class of directors, consisting of Mr. Klein, will expire at the third annual general meeting. CCXI will not hold an annual meeting of shareholders until after it consummates its initial business combination. Holders of the CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares have the right to appoint and remove all directors of the CCXI Board prior to consummation of the CCXI initial business combination and holders of the CCXI public shares will not have the right to vote on the appointment or removal of directors during such time. These provisions of the CCXI current articles of association may only be amended if approved by a special resolution passed by at least 90% (or, where such amendment is proposed in respect of the consummation of the CCXI initial business combination, two -thirds ) of the CCXI Ordinary Shares voting at the applicable general meeting, voting together as a single class. CCXI’s officers are appointed by the CCXI Board and serve at the discretion of the CCXI Board, rather than for specific terms of office. The CCXI Board is authorized to appoint persons to the offices set forth in the CCXI current articles of association as it deems appropriate. The CCXI current articles of association provide that CCXI’s officers may consist of any Chairman or Co -Chairman of the CCXI Board, a Vice Chairman of the CCXI Board, a Chief Executive Officer, a President, a Chief Financial Officer, a Secretary, a Treasurer, Vice Presidents, one or more assistant Vice Presidents, one or more assistant Treasurers, one or more assistant Secretaries and such other officers as may be determined by the CCXI Board. Committees of the Board of Directors The CCXI Board has two standing committees: an audit committee and a compensation committee. Both the audit committee and the compensation committee are composed solely of independent directors. Subject to phase -in rules and certain limited exceptions, the Nasdaq Rules and Rule 10A -3 of the Exchange Act require that the audit committee of a listed company be comprised solely of independent directors. In addition, the Nasdaq Rules generally require that the compensation committee of a listed company be comprised solely of independent directors, subject to certain limited exceptions set forth thereunder. Each committee operates under a charter that was approved by the CCXI Board and has the composition and responsibilities described below. The charter of each committee is available on our website. Audit Committee The members of the CCXI audit committee are Mr. Lapping, Mr. Murphy and Mr. Sherman. Under the Nasdaq Rules and applicable SEC rules, CCXI is required to have at least three members of the audit committee, all of whom must be independent, subject to the exception described below. Overview We are a blank check company incorporated in the Cayman Islands on June 4, 2025, formed for the purpose of effecting a business combination with one or more businesses. We intend to effectuate our business combination using cash derived from the proceeds of the CCXI IPO, the sale of the CCXI private placement units, our shares, debt or a combination of cash, shares and debt. The registration statement in connection with the CCXI IPO became effective on December 16, 2025. On December 18, 2025, we consummated our initial public offering of 41,400,000 CCXI public units, including 5,400,000 CCXI public units issued pursuant to the full exercise of the over -allotment option. Each CCXI public unit consists of one CCXI Class A Ordinary Share and one -tenth of a CCXI public warrant. The CCXI public units were sold at a price of $10.00 per CCXI public unit, generating gross proceeds to us of $414,000,000. Simultaneously with the closing of the CCXI IPO and pursuant to the Private Placement Units Purchase Agreement, we completed the sale of 500,000 CCXI private placement units to the Sponsor in the private placement at a purchase price of $10.00 per CCXI private placement unit, generating gross proceeds to us of $5,000,000. The CCXI private placement unit (and underlying securities) are identical to the CCXI public units (and underlying securities), except as otherwise disclosed in the section entitled “ Description of Securities ” of this proxy statement/prospectus. Following the closing of the CCXI IPO and private placement, an aggregate amount of $414,000,000 from the net proceeds of the CCXI IPO and private placement was initially placed in the trust account. The trust account may be invested only (i) in United States government securities within the meaning of Section 2(a)(16) of the Investment Company Act, having a maturity of 185 days or less, (ii) in money market funds meeting the conditions of paragraphs (d)(1), (d)(2), (d)(3) and (d)(4) of Rule 2a -7 promulgated under the Investment Company Act, which invest only in direct U.S. government treasury obligations, (iii) as uninvested cash or (iv) in an interest or non -interest bearing demand deposit account at a U.S. chartered commercial bank with consolidated assets of $100 billion or more selected by Continental that is reasonably satisfactory to us, until the earlier of: (x) the completion of the business combination or (y) the distribution of the trust account, as described below. We have until March 18, 2028 (27 months from the closing of the CCXI IPO since we have executed a definitive agreement for an initial business combination within 24 months from the closing of the CCXI IPO), or until such (x) earlier liquidation date as the CCXI Board may approve or (y) such later date as our shareholders may approve pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, to consummate an initial business combination. If we are unable to complete an initial business combination within 27 months from the closing of the CCXI IPO (such 27 month period, as may be amended, the “ completion window ”), we will (i) cease all operations except for the purpose of winding up, (ii) as promptly as reasonably possible, but not more than ten business days thereafter, redeem the CCXI public shares, at a per -share price, payable in cash, equal to the aggregate amount then on deposit in the trust account including interest earned on the funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals and less up to $100,000 of interest to pay dissolution expenses net of taxes payable, if any, divided by the number of then outstanding CCXI public shares, which redemption will completely extinguish CCXI public shareholders’ rights as shareholders (including the right to receive further liquidating distributions, if any), subject to applicable law, and (iii) as promptly as reasonably possible following such redemption, subject to the approval of our remaining shareholders and the CCXI Board, dissolve and liquidate, subject, in each case, to our obligations under Cayman Islands law to provide for claims of creditors and the requirements of other applicable law. 216 Table of Contents We may seek to extend the completion window consistent with applicable laws, regulations and stock exchange rules by amending the CCXI current articles of association. Any such amendment would require the approval of CCXI shareholders and the holders of CCXI public shares will be provided the opportunity to redeem all or a portion of their CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares in connection with the vote on such approval. Such redemptions will decrease the amount held in the trust account and our capitalization and may affect our ability to maintain our listing on Nasdaq. In addition, the Nasdaq rules require SPACs (such as us) to complete their initial business combination within 36 months. If we do not meet this requirement, our securities will likely be subject to suspension of trading and delisting from Nasdaq. Warrant Instruments We account for CCXI Warrants as either equity -classified or liability -classified instruments based on an assessment of the Warrant’s specific terms and applicable authoritative guidance in FASB ASC Topic 480, “Distinguishing Liabilities from Equity” (“ ASC 480 ”), and FASB ASC Topic 815, “Derivatives and Hedging” (“ ASC 815 ”). The assessment considers whether the CCXI Warrants are freestanding financial instruments pursuant to ASC 480, meet the definition of a liability pursuant to ASC 480, and whether the CCXI Warrants meet all of the requirements for equity classification under ASC 815, including whether the CCXI Warrants are indexed to our own Ordinary Shares and whether the CCXI Warrant holders could potentially require “net cash settlement” in a circumstance outside of our control, among other conditions for equity classification. This assessment, which requires the use of professional judgment, is conducted at the time of Warrant issuance and as of each subsequent quarterly period end date while the CCXI Warrants are outstanding. For issued or modified CCXI Warrants that meet all of the criteria for equity classification, the CCXI Warrants are required to be recorded as a component of additional paid -in capital at the time of issuance. For issued or modified CCXI Warrants that do not meet all of the criteria for equity classification, the Warrants are required to be recorded at their initial fair value on the date of issuance, and each condensed balance sheet date thereafter. Accordingly, we evaluated and classified the CCXI Warrant instruments under equity treatment at its assigned fair value. Net Loss Per Ordinary Share We comply with the accounting and disclosure requirements of FASB ASC Topic 260, “Earnings Per Share.” Net income per Ordinary Share is computed by dividing net loss applicable to CCXI shareholders by the weighted average number of CCXI Ordinary Shares outstanding for the applicable periods. We apply the two -class method in calculating earnings per CCXI Ordinary Share and allocate net loss pro rata to CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares subject to possible redemption, nonredeemable CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares and CCXI Class B Ordinary Shares. Accretion associated with the redeemable CCXI Class A Ordinary Shares is excluded from earnings per share as the redemption value is not in excess of the fair value. The global economy depends on millions of workers performing physically demanding tasks every day. Across manufacturing facilities, warehouses and distribution centers, workers move materials, replenish inventory, transport goods and perform countless repetitive workflows that are essential to modern industrial operations. While industrial automation has transformed many aspects of production over the past several decades, a substantial portion of this work continues to rely on human labor. At the same time, the supply of available labor is becoming increasingly constrained. Demographic shifts, an aging workforce, continued growth in e -commerce and the reshoring of manufacturing have created a structural imbalance between labor supply and demand that is expected to persist for years to come. In the United States alone, approximately 409,000 manufacturing positions were unfilled in 2025, and that shortage is projected to increase to approximately 1.9 million positions by 2033 if current workforce trends continue. Similar workforce shortages continue to affect warehouse and distribution operations, where employers face ongoing challenges attracting and retaining workers for physically demanding roles. We believe that these long -term labor dynamics are reshaping how industrial companies think about workforce planning, operational resilience and automation. Industrial companies have responded by investing heavily in automation technologies, including fixed industrial robots, automated storage and retrieval systems, conveyors and autonomous mobile robots. These technologies have delivered significant productivity improvements and remain essential components of modern manufacturing and logistics operations. However, they are generally designed to automate specific, highly structured workflows within dedicated operating environments. Many physical tasks continue to rely on people because they require mobility, manipulation and adaptability within dynamic environments that were designed for human workers rather than machines. Management estimates the near -term addressable market for humanoid robots across manufacturing, distribution and logistics environments in the United States to be approximately $1 trillion. We believe that these industries represent the initial opportunity for humanoid robotics because they combine persistent labor shortages, repetitive physical workflows and measurable customer return on investment. Humanoids: the next frontier of industrial automation. We believe the next generation of industrial automation will be built around the world that already exists. Factories, warehouses, shelving systems, tools and material flows have all been designed for people. Rather than requiring customers to redesign these environments around automation, humanoid robots have the potential to operate within existing infrastructure while performing a broad range of physical tasks. We believe that this human -centric approach carries advantages of existing investments, reduces deployment complexity and enables customers to automate work with substantially greater flexibility than traditional single -purpose automation systems. We believe the ability to automate physical labor is becoming increasingly important to both economic and national competitiveness. As countries seek to strengthen domestic manufacturing, improve supply chain resilience and address structural labor shortages, we believe that humanoid robotics has the potential to become an important enabling technology for the next generation of industrial production. Unlike conventional automation, which is typically designed to perform a single task within a highly structured environment, humanoid robots combine mobility, manipulation and artificial intelligence into a general -purpose system capable of performing multiple workflows. Humanoids are designed to work with humans, other traditional automation machines, other robotic solutions ( e.g., AMRs), as well as other humanoids. We believe that this flexibility enables customers to automate a broader range of physical work while increasing robot utilization as the platform acquires new capabilities over time. Agility has deliberately focused its initial commercial deployments on manufacturing, distribution and logistics, which we refer to as our beachhead markets. These industries combine persistent labor shortages, repetitive physical workflows and environments already designed around human workers, making them an ideal entry point for humanoid robotics. Today, Digit is primarily deployed in repetitive physical roles that customers often struggle to fill due to ongoing hiring and retention challenges. By helping customers address these labor gaps, we believe that Agility is able to deliver measurable customer return on investment while enabling employees to focus on higher -value activities. 225 Table of Contents Over time, we expect continued advancements in embodied AI, manipulation and cooperative safety to enable Digit to perform an expanding range of workflows across existing customer facilities before extending into adjacent industries and entirely new end markets. Ultimately, we believe customers are seeking to invest in useful physical labor  solutions. As Agility continues to evolve through engineering innovation and broad commercial adoption of Digit, we believe customer value and the addressable market for humanoid robotics will continue to expand. These deployments demonstrate Digit’s ability to perform useful physical labor in demanding industrial environments while generating the operational experience that continues to shape the evolution of our platform. Experience gained through customer deployments has directly informed the evolution of Digit. Rather than defining our product roadmap solely through engineering objectives, we have prioritized the capabilities customers identified as most important for broader commercial adoption. To support this strategy, Agility established the Customer Acceleration Program (“ CAP ”) in late 2025, a structured commercialization framework designed to move customers from initial evaluation to scaled deployment. Participation in CAP requires customers to pay a program fee of approximately $500,000 to Agility, reflecting a meaningful commercial commitment to evaluating deployment of Digit within their operations. As of May 2026, Agility has signed four new customers to the CAP and was engaged with more than 30 prospective customers through active commercial discussions and the CAP. Each customer deployment also generates valuable operational intelligence that strengthens our platform. We believe that this repeatable commercialization framework, combined with growing customer demand and our commercial deployment experience, positions Agility to accelerate the commercial adoption of humanoid robotics across manufacturing, distribution and logistics. A Platform Purpose-Built for Commercial Deployment Commercializing humanoid robotics begins with safety. Today’s humanoid robots must generally remain confined to workcells or other safety barriers that create physical separation from humans. While recent advances in artificial intelligence have significantly expanded what humanoid robots are capable of accomplishing, broad commercial adoption depends on enabling robots to safely operate alongside people in active industrial environments. We therefore believe safety, in addition to artificial intelligence and highly sophisticated robotics hardware, is an important limiting factor to broad scaling of the humanoid robotics industry. Years of deployment alongside leading enterprise customers reinforced this conclusion. As Digit was deployed within our customers’ facilities, we gained unique firsthand insight into the operational and safety requirements customers expect before deploying industrial automation at scale. These deployments demonstrated that broad adoption requires more than intelligent software or capable hardware — it requires a trustworthy and certifiable safety architecture that enables humanoid robots to work productively alongside people in real -world operating environments. Our experience also highlighted that many of the most critical safety requirements only emerge through live deployments, where customer expectations, insurance requirements and operational realities intersect. This philosophy fundamentally shaped the development of Digit v5. Rather than treating safety as a feature, Digit v5 was redesigned from the ground up with cooperative safety as a foundational design objective. We define cooperative safety as the ability for humanoid robots to safely operate alongside people without relying on traditional workcells or physical safety barriers. Achieving this capability required integrating safety throughout the robot’s mechanical architecture, sensing systems, controls, software and operating behavior, creating a unified system designed for operation alongside human coworkers. We believe safety cannot be added to a humanoid robot as a standalone feature — it must be designed into every aspect of the system from the outset. We believe the ability to operate safely outside of traditional safety cages represents one of the most important milestones in the evolution of industrial humanoid robotics. As industry standards for human -robot collaboration continue to develop, we are actively engaged with customers, technology partners and standards bodies to help define the frameworks and performance requirements necessary for deployment in shared workspaces. Our objective is to enable Digit to operate productively in close proximity to people while meeting the safety, reliability and certification standards required by enterprise customers. This integrated approach to safety extends across the entire Agility platform. Purpose -built robotics, embodied AI, deployment software and our proprietary cooperative safety architecture work together as a unified system to enable Digit to operate safely and productively within real -world customer environments. The platform is informed 227 Table of Contents by commercial operating data generated through customer deployments, allowing us to continually refine safety performance and real -world operating behavior. This integrated approach differentiates Digit v5 from conventional humanoid designs and establishes the foundation for broader commercial adoption. The following sections describe how each component of our integrated platform contributes to that objective. Safe physical labor requires an integrated system. Delivering useful physical labor safely and reliably requires more than a capable humanoid robot. It requires robotics, embodied AI and deployment software working together as a unified technology platform. Agility has spent more than a decade developing these capabilities in parallel, designing each component to operate as part of an integrated system rather than as standalone technologies. Commercial deployments continuously strengthen the platform by generating operational data that improves embodied AI, informs future hardware development and enables software enhancements to be deployed across customer fleets through Agility Arc. Our integrated technology platform consists of three tightly interwoven components: • Digit , our purpose -built humanoid robot designed to perform useful physical labor in environments built for people. • Embodied AI , our proprietary software stack that enables Digit to perceive, reason, navigate, manipulate objects and execute increasingly complex physical tasks. • Agility Arc , our cloud -based deployment and fleet management platform that manages robot operations, workflow orchestration, analytics and over -the-air software updates. Together, Digit, embodied AI and Agility Arc form a vertically integrated technology platform that enables Agility to design, deploy and continuously improve humanoid robots performing useful physical labor. Digit: designed for useful physical labor. Delivering useful physical labor begins with physics. Before a robot can understand its environment through embodied AI or safely operate alongside people, it must first possess the physical capability to perform the work. Dynamic stability, locomotion, manipulation, strength, power efficiency and reliability are fundamental engineering challenges that must be solved before a humanoid robot can become commercially useful. Agility’s technology draws on more than a decade of research and development originating at the Oregon State University Robotics Institute and DARPA -funded programs. Agility did not set out simply to build a humanoid robot. The Company’s early work focused on understanding how animals and people move, applying first principles of biomechanics and robotics to reproduce those same physical capabilities through engineered systems. This work resulted in Cassie (2016), a commercially available research robot that validated many of the foundational technologies required for dynamic locomotion and physical interaction with the world. Building on those capabilities, Agility introduced Digit v1 (2017) as its first humanoid proof of concept, demonstrating how those foundational technologies could be applied within environments designed for people. As these scientific and engineering challenges were solved, Agility’s focus shifted from proving what was technically possible to understanding how those capabilities could solve meaningful customer problems. Rather than assuming where humanoid robots would create the greatest value, Agility evaluated hundreds of potential workflows across a broad range of industries and applications. Those learnings ultimately identified manufacturing, distribution and logistics as our beachhead markets. The result was Digit, a general -purpose humanoid robot engineered to perform useful physical labor within environments built for people. Digit’s physical architecture is the product of first -principles engineering. Rather than designing a robot to resemble a person, we engineered the machine required to solve real customer problems. Four core design principles shaped Digit’s architecture: • Dynamic Stability. A dynamically balanced bipedal design enables Digit to navigate narrow aisles, hallways and other crowded, changing environments while moving naturally through spaces designed for people. 228 Table of Contents • Upright Architecture. An upright torso minimizes the robot’s footprint while optimizing balance and providing an efficient location for onboard computing, battery systems and sensors. • High -Mounted Manipulation. Shoulder -mounted , bimanual manipulation maximizes reach, enables lifting and repositioning of large objects, and improves whole -body coordination, stability and recovery during operation. • Human -Aware Design. Human -robot interaction features, including a face with expressive signaling, enable Digit to communicate intent intuitively and operate naturally alongside people. Together, these engineering decisions naturally resulted in a humanoid form factor — not because our objective was to replicate human anatomy, but because it proved to be the most effective architecture for performing useful physical labor in environments designed for people. The culmination of this work was Digit v4 (2025), Agility’s first commercially deployed humanoid robot designed to perform useful physical labor in real -world customer environments. Designed specifically for manufacturing, distribution and logistics, Digit v4 features a 35 -pound carrying capacity, four -hour runtime with autonomous charging, 360 -degree sensing awareness, adaptive dexterity designed for industrial workflows, deployments that have passed OSHA recognized NRTL field evaluation, and next -generation power -efficient edge AI compute. These commercial deployments validated the core platform while providing the operational experience that directly shaped the development of Digit v5. Customer deployments consistently reinforced four priorities for broader commercial adoption: the ability to operate safely alongside people, maximize utilization across multiple shifts, handle heavier payloads and perform a broader range of workflows within a facility. Digit v5 was engineered to address each of these requirements through several significant advancements from Digit v4, including: • Cooperative Safety .    A purpose -built cooperative safety architecture designed to enable operation alongside people outside traditional robotic workcells. • Proprietary Fast -Charge Battery System. Approximately 20 hours of operation within a 24 -hour period through an industry -leading 10:1 charge ratio, significantly increasing robot utilization across multiple shifts. • Expanded Payload Capacity. Approximately 40% greater payload capacity, enabling Digit to lift up to 50 pounds and automate a broader range of industrial workflows. • Greater Reach. Approximately 30% greater vertical reach to 7.2 feet, expanding the range of storage locations, workstations and material handling applications Digit can access. • Modular End Effectors. Interchangeable end effectors that enable customers to configure Digit for different applications and perform multiple workflows throughout a facility. Underlying Digit’s performance is a small number of highly integrated proprietary systems, including its cycloidal actuators, modular manipulation system, sensor architecture, battery technology and control systems. Agility has developed these core technologies specifically for the demands of humanoid robotics, enabling high performance, durability and reliability in demanding industrial environments. Controlling these critical systems also provides a foundation for future product innovation while giving Agility greater control over manufacturing, supply chain, product reliability and long -term cost reduction as the platform scales. Embodied AI: Agility owns the physical AI layer. Embodied AI is the intelligence layer that enables Digit to perceive, reason and interact with the physical world. While recent advances in artificial intelligence have dramatically improved a robot’s ability to understand language, images and its surroundings, performing useful physical labor requires a fundamentally different form of intelligence. Agility refers to this capability as physical AI, and we have developed a proprietary embodied AI stack that enables Digit to move, manipulate objects and perform useful physical labor within real -world customer environments. 229 Table of Contents Agility owns this physical AI layer. Our proprietary embodied AI stack combines perception, locomotion, manipulation, motion planning and controls into a unified intelligence system that enables Digit to operate autonomously within complex industrial environments. Working together with Digit’s purpose -built hardware and Agility Arc, embodied AI transforms a capable machine into an autonomous worker capable of performing increasingly sophisticated physical tasks. Physical AI and semantic AI solve fundamentally different problems. Semantic AI systems, including large language models and vision foundation models, are trained on publicly available text, images and video, enabling robots to recognize objects, understand language and interpret their surroundings. These technologies are becoming increasingly accessible across the industry, and we expect continued advances in semantic AI to benefit the broader robotics ecosystem. Physical AI, however, must solve an entirely different challenge: determining how a specific robot should move, balance, manipulate objects and interact safely with the physical world. Unlike semantic AI, there is no public dataset that provides the correct motor commands, control policies or physical behaviors required to operate a humanoid robot. These capabilities must be developed specifically for the robot itself. Developing physical AI therefore requires a fundamentally different approach to training. Agility combines learning from demonstration — including teleoperation, motion capture and simulated examples — with reinforcement learning, allowing Digit to refine behaviors through repeated practice in simulation before deployment into customer environments. Over time, these capabilities are expected to continue improving through learning across fleets of deployed robots. Commercial deployment is central to the continued advancement of our embodied AI. Every Digit operating in a customer facility generates proprietary operational data that strengthens existing behaviors, supports the development of new skills and expands the range of physical work the platform can perform. We believe ownership of the physical AI layer represents one of Agility’s most important competitive advantages. As commercial deployments continue to expand, our embodied AI platform becomes increasingly capable, strengthening Digit’s performance, expanding commercially viable applications and reinforcing Agility’s leadership in useful physical labor. Agility Arc: The operating system for commercial deployment. Agility Arc is our cloud -based software platform that connects Digit with customer operations. As humanoid robot deployments expand from individual robots to enterprise -scale fleets, software becomes essential for coordinating robot activity, integrating with existing customer workflows and managing operations across multiple facilities. Together with Digit and our embodied AI platform, Agility Arc serves as the operational layer of the Agility platform. Agility Arc coordinates every stage of robot deployment and operation. The platform assigns robots to workflows, monitors fleet performance, tracks robot health and enables over -the-air software updates, remote diagnostics and teleoperation when required. Arc also integrates with warehouse management systems, manufacturing execution systems and other forms of industrial automation, allowing Digit to operate as part of existing customer operations rather than as a standalone system. This integration reduces deployment complexity while enabling customers to scale humanoid robot fleets within their existing operating environments. Agility Arc also serves as the data layer for the Agility platform. Operational data generated by every deployed Digit flows through Arc, providing customers with visibility into fleet utilization, workflow performance and operational efficiency while enabling Agility to continuously improve its embodied AI platform. As commercial deployments expand, Arc becomes the mechanism through which real -world operating experience is collected, analyzed and translated into future software capabilities, new robot skills and product improvements. Beyond supporting Digit deployments, we believe Agility Arc has the potential to become an increasingly valuable enterprise software platform in its own right. Because Arc already integrates with warehouse management systems and other forms of industrial automation, we believe its capabilities can expand over time to help customers orchestrate broader automation environments beyond humanoid robots. This creates an opportunity to deepen customer relationships while further strengthening the connection between commercial deployment, operational intelligence and continuous platform improvement. 230 Table of Contents Commercial deployment creates a compounding advantage. We believe that one of Agility’s most significant long -term competitive advantages is the continuous learning generated through commercial deployment. Unlike traditional industrial automation systems, which are designed to perform fixed tasks throughout their operating lives, Digit is designed to become increasingly capable over time. Every commercial deployment generates proprietary operational data that strengthens our embodied AI, informs future hardware development and expands the capabilities of the platform. Commercial deployments expose Digit to diverse customer facilities, workflows, environmental conditions and human interactions that cannot be fully replicated through laboratory testing or simulation. This real -world operating experience improves perception, manipulation, mobility and task execution while expanding our understanding of how humanoid robots perform useful physical labor in dynamic industrial environments. We believe that this creates a compounding competitive advantage. Operational data generated through commercial deployments strengthens embodied AI, enabling Digit to perform a broader range of workflows and increasing the value of every deployment. As customers expand deployments across additional facilities and applications, Agility collects more operational data, creating a powerful data flywheel that continuously strengthens the platform. Unlike traditional industrial automation, where product development largely precedes commercialization, the commercialization of humanoid robotics and product development occur simultaneously. As our installed base continues to grow, we expect this cycle of deployment, learning and capability expansion to accelerate. We believe the companies that deploy the most robots performing useful physical labor will ultimately develop the most capable physical AI platforms. Commercial deployment is therefore not the end of product development — it is the engine that drives it. Cooperative Safety: an integrated architecture. Cooperative safety is the culmination of Agility’s integrated technology platform. Rather than viewing safety as a standalone feature, we designed Digit v5 around a unified architecture in which robotics, embodied AI, controls, sensing and deployment software work together to enable safe operation alongside people. We believe cooperative safety cannot be achieved by adding individual sensors or software features to an existing robot. Instead, it must be designed into every layer of the system from the outset. We believe that Digit’s physical architecture provides the foundation for cooperative safety. Dynamic stability, human -aware design and purpose -built hardware enable the robot to move predictably within environments designed for people. Building on this foundation, our embodied AI continuously interprets the surrounding environment, identifies people and objects, plans safe motions and adapts to changing operating conditions in real time. Agility Arc complements these capabilities by monitoring robot health, deploying software updates and providing operational oversight across customer fleets. Together, these systems enable Digit to operate safely while maintaining the flexibility required for useful physical labor. Rather than limiting robots to isolated workcells performing fixed tasks, cooperative safety enables Digit to move throughout customer facilities, transition between workflows and operate alongside human coworkers. This expands robot utilization, improves customer economics and significantly broadens the range of commercially viable applications for humanoid robotics. Cooperative safety also reflects years of commercial experience. Deployments across manufacturing, distribution and logistics environments provided firsthand insight into the operational and safety requirements enterprise customers expect before deploying automation at scale. Those learnings directly informed the development of Digit v5, which was redesigned from the ground up with cooperative safety as a foundational design objective. We believe broad commercial adoption of humanoid robotics will require robots to operate safely alongside people without traditional robotic safety cells or significant facility modifications. Digit v4 deployments have passed OSHA -recognized NRTL field evaluations, and Digit v5 builds on that foundation through a purpose -built cooperative safety architecture designed specifically for shared work environments. We believe the regulatory framework governing humanoid robotics will continue to evolve as commercial deployment accelerates, and that Agility’s commercial experience and integrated approach to cooperative safety position us to help shape the standards that enable safe, large -scale deployment. 231 Table of Contents A Flexible Business Model with Attractive Economics Flexible adoption models. Agility’s business model is designed to commercialize useful physical labor through flexible customer adoption models that generate compelling customer returns while supporting attractive long -term economics for the Company. We offer two primary commercial models that allow customers to align their investment with their operational objectives, capital planning processes and stage of automation adoption. Under our Robot -as-a-Service (“ RaaS ”) model, Agility retains ownership of Digit while customers pay a recurring subscription fee that includes the robot, software and ongoing support services. This model lowers the barriers to adoption by reducing upfront capital requirements, simplifying deployment and allowing customers to integrate humanoid robotics into their operations with minimal initial investment. We believe this model is particularly attractive for customers because it provides an economically attractive alternative to conventional labor costs while allowing them to address critical labor shortages and difficult -to-fill operational roles. As of May 2026, the $300 million of contracted Digit v5 orders were structured under our RaaS model, which indicates a strong customer preference for recurring, low -friction adoption of humanoid robotics. Customers may also acquire Digit through a traditional ownership model, under which the customer purchases the robot while continuing to subscribe to software and support services. We believe the ownership model may appeal to larger organizations with sophisticated automation programs that prefer to acquire and manage strategic automation assets directly. This model may become increasingly attractive as humanoid robotics becomes more broadly established within customers’ long -term automation strategies and capital investment programs. Together, these complementary commercial models allow Agility to meet customers wherever they are in their automation journey while creating long -term customer relationships under either adoption model. Measurable customer ROI. Agility believes customer adoption begins with measurable economic value. Our commercial models are designed to deliver compelling customer returns from the outset of deployment by addressing persistent labor shortages in roles that customers often struggle to fill. Today, Digit is primarily deployed to perform repetitive physical tasks where employers face ongoing hiring and retention challenges, enabling customers to improve productivity while augmenting their existing workforce. Under the RaaS model, subscription pricing is generally structured at a discount to a customer’s fully burdened labor cost, allowing customers to realize a positive economic return immediately upon deployment while avoiding significant upfront capital investment. Because customers are often deploying Digit into positions that are difficult to staff consistently, the economic benefit extends beyond direct labor savings and may also include improved operational continuity, reduced overstaffing requirements and increased production capacity. This approach enables customers to adopt humanoid robotics with minimal financial friction through a flexible operating expense model while addressing critical labor gaps. Customers choosing to purchase Digit also benefit from compelling economics. Based on our current planning assumptions, Digit v5 is expected to achieve customer breakeven in approximately 1.1 years. We believe this payback period compares favorably to many industrial automation investments and reflects the value created by deploying Digit into labor -constrained workflows where productivity, uptime and workforce availability are key drivers of customer returns. Under either commercial model, customers have the opportunity to generate meaningful long -term savings while benefiting from increased operational flexibility, improved productivity and continued software enhancements that expand the capabilities of the platform throughout its operating life. Compelling lifetime unit economics. Both commercial models are designed to generate attractive lifetime economics for Agility while supporting durable, recurring customer relationships. Illustrative projected unit economics under each commercial model, including expected revenue, capital recovery periods and margin assumptions, are presented under “Unaudited Prospective Unit Economics Information.” 232 Table of Contents Under the RaaS model, Agility generates recurring subscription revenue throughout the robot’s operating life while retaining ownership of the asset. Based on our current planning assumptions, a single Digit deployment is expected to generate approximately $500,000 of cumulative revenue over an assumed five -year useful life while enabling Agility to recover its invested capital in less than one year. Under the ownership model, a larger portion of revenue is recognized at the time of robot delivery, followed by recurring software and support revenue throughout the robot’s operating life. Based on our current planning assumptions, a single Digit deployment under this model is expected to generate approximately $400,000 of cumulative revenue over the same five -year period. Our economic model strengthens as the business scales. Continued improvements in product design, bill of materials optimization, manufacturing efficiency and supply chain scale are expected to reduce product costs while improving capital efficiency under the RaaS model. At the same time, growth in our installed base is expected to increase recurring software and service revenue, while continued improvements in Digit’s capabilities create opportunities to deliver additional customer value over time. Together, these factors provide a potential path toward product gross margins in excess of 70% as the business scales. Achieving these improvements depends on Agility’s ability to continuously improve manufacturing efficiency while reducing product costs at scale.
