Our capabilities include U.S. -based production, integrated engineering and manufacturing, proprietary technologies and supply chain capabilities that enable us to manufacture, deploy and continuously improve Digit as production volumes increase. This infrastructure provides the foundation for scaling production while continuously improving product quality, manufacturing efficiency and cost. The following sections describe the principal components of Agility’s industrial infrastructure and how they support the commercial deployment of humanoid robotics. RoboFab is a full-scale humanoid factory. RoboFab is our humanoid manufacturing facility and serves as the foundation of Agility’s commercial -scale production. Located in Salem, Oregon, RoboFab was designed specifically for the manufacturing of humanoid robots. The facility utilizes a modular manufacturing architecture that enables production to scale efficiently while supporting continuous improvements in quality, productivity and cost. Importantly, RoboFab is not a future capability — it is operating today and producing Digit robots for deployment. The facility has a designed production capacity of up to 10,000 robots annually and was built to enable production capacity to expand efficiently with relatively modest incremental capital investment. This approach provides Agility with the manufacturing foundation required to support increasing commercial deployment while maintaining the flexibility to accommodate future generations of Digit. 233 Table of Contents Beyond production capacity, RoboFab provides a platform for continuous operational improvement. As manufacturing experience grows, Agility is able to refine production processes, optimize its supply chain and implement engineering -driven improvements that enhance product quality, reduce manufacturing costs and strengthen customer economics over time. Engineering and manufacturing as one system. Agility tightly integrates engineering and manufacturing, with product engineers working directly alongside production teams on the RoboFab factory floor. This close collaboration creates a continuous feedback loop between product design, manufacturing and commercial deployment, allowing product and manufacturing improvements to be identified, implemented and validated rapidly. Manufacturing experience provides valuable insights into product design, assembly processes, component performance and supply chain efficiency. By embedding engineering within the manufacturing environment, Agility continuously improves manufacturability, product quality and cost while accelerating the introduction of future product generations. Well-developed strategic supply chain. Agility has established a supply chain designed to support commercial -scale production. Approximately 75% of Digit’s components are currently sourced from suppliers in the United States, providing greater control over quality, logistics and production while supporting a resilient domestic manufacturing footprint. This domestic supply chain also positions Agility to support broader U.S. manufacturing priorities while reducing dependence on global supply chains. As production volumes increase, Agility expects to continue strengthening its supply chain through strategic sourcing, supplier collaboration and purchasing scale. Together, these initiatives are expected to improve component availability, reduce manufacturing costs and support the long -term commercialization of humanoid robotics. Proprietary hardware and systems. Agility has developed, or secured exclusive rights within the humanoid robotics sector to, several of the critical hardware systems that define Digit’s performance. These systems include Digit’s actuators, manipulation architecture, sensing systems and battery technology. By controlling these critical technologies, Agility is designed to be able to optimize product performance, reliability, manufacturability and cost while reducing dependence on commercially available components. Digit’s proprietary cycloidal actuators are the most significant example and represent one of Agility’s core technical differentiators. Agility has developed substantial intellectual property around these actuators, which are designed specifically for the repeated impacts, dynamic stability and precise force control required in humanoid robotics. Their durability and efficiency support Digit’s ability to operate reliably in demanding industrial environments, while Agility’s control of the underlying technology enables continued optimization of performance, manufacturing cost and future product generations. Agility also has exclusive rights within the humanoid robotics sector to certain licensed technologies, including its fast -charge battery system, further strengthening its control over critical product capabilities without requiring every component to be developed internally. A proven cost reduction roadmap. One of the most important drivers of Agility’s long -term financial performance is the ability to continuously reduce the cost of Digit as production scales. The attractive unit economics discussed in the previous section — including capital payback periods of less than one year under our RaaS model and a path toward product gross margins in excess of 70%–are supported by our ability to improve product design, optimize manufacturing processes and strengthen our supply chain over time. Importantly, Agility does not view cost reduction as primarily a function of higher production volumes. While manufacturing scale contributes to lower costs, we believe the greatest opportunities come from engineering improvements, supplier engagement and manufacturing experience. These initiatives simplify manufacturing, reduce component costs and improve production efficiency while simultaneously enhancing product performance. 234 Table of Contents This is not a capability we are forecasting for the first time. Through engineering improvements, supplier engagement, manufacturing experience and increasing production scale, Agility has already reduced the bill of materials for Digit v4 to approximately $125,000 per robot. These same operating disciplines are now being applied to Digit v5. Digit v5 is not a concept or a design on paper. We have already built and produced Digit v5 prototype units, which we expect to release in late 2026, and our early manufacturing experience is validating the cost reduction roadmap developed for the platform. While meaningful cost reductions have already been achieved, we continue to identify additional opportunities across engineering, supply chain and manufacturing that we believe will substantially reduce the bill of materials over time. We believe that this repeatable process of engineering innovation, manufacturing learning and supply chain optimization will continue to strengthen both customer economics and Agility’s long -term financial performance. Overview Agility Robotics, Inc. was founded in 2015 out of the Oregon State University Robotics Institute with initial funding from DARPA and has spent more than a decade advancing humanoids into real -world commercial deployment. Headquartered in Salem, Oregon, our mission is to build robot partners that augment the human workforce, ultimately enabling humans to be more human. Agility’s solutions include Digit, a multi -purpose humanoid robot made for logistics and manufacturing work, and Agility Arc, a cloud automation platform for deploying and managing fleets of Digits. Agility is one of the only humanoid companies with multiple years of operational experience in real customer environments. Digit v4 is performing useful work today for leading enterprises including Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Amazon, with new deployments underway with large blue -chip customers. Digit v5, planned for launch in 2026, is designed as the world’s first AI -enabled cooperatively safe humanoid. Complementing Digit, Agility Arc, our cloud -based automation platform, is designed to integrate Digit into customer workflows, manage fleets, and optimize operations. Our differentiated business model deploys Digit through both robot deployment arrangements and ownership models, providing customers with flexible adoption paths. The robot deployment model generates recurring revenue streams over an estimated five -year useful life, while building strong customer retention. We have built RoboFab, the world’s first full -scale humanoid manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, designed to produce up to 10,000 Digits annually. Approximately 75% of Digit parts are currently sourced from the U.S., providing cost and availability advantages and supporting domestic manufacturing priorities. We develop our highest -value hardware systems in -house , including proprietary actuators, modular end effectors, whole -body control platform, sensor architecture, system -wide safety, and long -life quick -charge battery configuration. Our proprietary physical AI layer — combining learned skills, real -time coordination, and physics -based control — provides scaling performance and cost advantages over competitors reliant on third -party systems. We believe our domestic supply chain and vertically integrated manufacturing approach provides significant competitive advantages in terms of cost, supply security, and production scalability. Recent Developments The Merger Agreement On June 24, 2026, Agility entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger and Reorganization (as amended, modified, supplemented or waived from time to time, the “ Merger Agreement ”) with Churchill Capital Corp XI (“ CCXI ”), a Cayman Islands exempted company, and BLB Merger Sub, Inc., a Delaware corporation and direct, wholly -owned subsidiary of CCXI (“ Merger Sub ”). The Merger Agreement, among other things and subject to the terms and conditions contained therein, provides for (a) the transfer of the registration of CCXI by way of continuation from the Cayman Islands to the State of Delaware (the “ Domestication ”), and (b) following the Domestication, the merger of Merger Sub with and into Agility, with Agility continuing as the surviving corporation, and as a direct wholly owned subsidiary of CCXI (the “ Merger ,” and together with the Domestication 239 Table of Contents and the other transactions contemplated by the Merger Agreement and the related agreements, the “ Transactions ” or the “ business combination ”). In connection with the business combination, CCXI will change its name to “Agility Robotics, Inc.” While the legal acquirer in the Merger Agreement is CCXI, for financial accounting and reporting purposes under GAAP, Agility will be the accounting acquirer, CCXI will be treated as the “acquired” company, and the business combination will be accounted for as a “reverse recapitalization.” In accordance with this accounting method, the business combination will be treated as the equivalent of Agility issuing stock for the net assets of CCXI, accompanied by a recapitalization. The net assets of CCXI will be stated at historical cost, which are expected to approximate fair value, with no goodwill or other intangible assets recorded, and operations prior to the business combination will be those of Agility. Upon the completion of the business combination, Agility will become the successor registrant with the SEC, which means that Agility’s financial statements for previous periods will be presented in future periodic reports filed with the SEC. The most significant change to Agility’s financial position is expected to be an estimated increase in cash of approximately $ million, assuming maximum redemptions from CCXI’s shareholders (assuming approximately 100% of public shares redeemed), or approximately $          million assuming no redemptions of CCXI’s public shares, in each case including $201 million in gross proceeds from the PIPE Investment. Total direct and incremental transaction costs of CCXI related to the business combination are estimated at approximately $46 million and pro forma financial statements for the year -ended December 31, 2025 will include the reversal of $0.5 million of investment income related to the investments held in the CCXI trust account. In addition, as a consequence of being a public company, we will need to hire additional personnel and implement procedures and processes to address public company regulatory requirements and customary practices. We expect to incur additional annual expenses as a public company including, among other things, directors’ and officers’ liability insurance, director fees, and additional internal and external accounting, legal, and administrative resources, including increased audit and legal fees. Funding In July 2026, we authorized up to $100 million of additional financing through the issuance and sale of simple agreements for future equity (“ SAFEs ”), which we expect to convert into approximately 1,348,000 shares of Agility common stock. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, we have raised $100 million through the issuance and sale of such Agility SAFEs. The round was backed by a blend of strategic and institutional investors. We are utilizing the proceeds to accelerate deployments, Digit v5 production, and support the next phase of our growth. Trends and Key Factors Affecting Performance We believe that our performance and future success depend on several factors that present significant opportunities for us but also pose risks and challenges, including those discussed below and in the section of this proxy statement/prospectus titled “ Risk Factors. ” Development, Testing and Commercialization of Future Products Our future operating performance will depend on the successful commercialization of our next generation humanoid robots, Digit v5, which we currently expect to begin in 2027. Agility expects to continue investing significantly in research and development, engineering, manufacturing readiness, and commercialization activities with respect to Digit v5 and future products. The timing of future commercial launches, customer deployments, and revenue generation will depend on a number of factors, including continued product development, manufacturing readiness, supply chain execution, and successful customer implementation. These investments and the timing of commercialization will continue to influence our operating results, capital requirements, and growth expectations. Customer Adoption and Demand Our long -term growth depends on broader customer adoption of humanoid robotics across warehouse, logistics, manufacturing, and other commercial environments. Because humanoid robotics represents an emerging category within industrial automation, customer purchasing decisions, deployment timelines, and long -term adoption rates remain difficult to predict. 240 Table of Contents We expect robot deployment arrangements to become an increasingly important component of our commercialization strategy by reducing customers’ upfront investment while providing greater deployment flexibility and recurring revenue opportunities. The pace of customer adoption, commercial deployments, and expansion of robot deployment arrangements will be important drivers of our future operating performance. Manufacturing and Deployment Scale Our ability to meet anticipated demand depends on successfully scaling manufacturing and deployment operations while maintaining product quality, reliability, and cost discipline. We intend to continue to invest in manufacturing capabilities, production processes, supplier relationships, and deployment infrastructure to support future growth. Our operations rely on the availability of specialized components, materials, and manufacturing capacity. Supply chain constraints, production inefficiencies, component shortages, quality issues, or deployment delays could increase costs, delay customer implementations, and adversely affect our operating results. Continued Investment and Innovation We believe that we are a pioneer in the robotic systems industry and benefit from lessons learned over ten years and extensive research and development investment in our proprietary technologies and our extensive patent portfolio. However, our financial performance is significantly dependent on our ability to maintain this leading position and further dependent on the investments we make in research and development. It is essential that we continually identify and respond to rapidly evolving customer requirements, develop and introduce innovative new products, enhance and service existing products and generate active market demand for our robotic systems. If we fail to do this, our market position and revenue may be adversely affected, and our investments in these technologies will not be recovered. Regulatory Environment and Compliance Our business operates within an evolving legal and regulatory environment as commercial deployment of robotics and AI Technologies continues to expand. We are subject to a variety of federal, state, and international laws and regulations relating to product and workplace safety, environmental matters, export controls, cybersecurity, data privacy, intellectual property, employment matters, and other regulatory requirements. As our commercial operations grow, we expect our compliance obligations and related costs to increase. In addition, evolving laws, regulations, and industry standards governing robotics, AI, and workplace automation may require changes to our products, deployment practices, or business processes. We continue to invest in our legal, compliance, cybersecurity, and governance capabilities to support our growth and public company obligations; however, changes in the regulatory landscape or our ability to comply with applicable requirements could increase operating costs, delay customer deployments, or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Components of Results of Operations Net sales Our commercialization strategy is designed to support customers throughout the adoption lifecycle through multiple complementary revenue streams. Net sales are primarily generated through direct sales of Digit humanoid robots and related ancillary hardware, robot deployment arrangements, Customer Acceleration Program (“ CAP ”) engagements, and ongoing support services. Sales of Robotics Equipment Revenue from robotics equipment consists primarily of sales of Digit humanoid robots and related ancillary hardware to customers for their owned use. Revenue from robot sales is recognized at a point in time when control of the robot transfers to the customer, generally upon completion of substantive customer acceptance procedures. Certain robot sale arrangements also include training and software support, which are recognized separately as the related services are provided. 241 Table of Contents Deployment and Professional Services Under our robot deployment model, we deploy Digit robots at customer facilities while retaining ownership of the robots and provide customers with access to the deployed systems together with related monitoring, maintenance, software, and support over a defined service term. Revenue is generally recognized ratably over the contractual service period beginning when the deployed robot is operational. While we continue to support direct robot sales where appropriate based on customer requirements and deployment objectives, we expect robot deployment model to become an increasingly important component of our long -term commercialization strategy as it allows customers to deploy robots without a significant upfront capital investment while providing the Company with a recurring revenue stream and ongoing customer engagement. Other professional service revenue is primarily driven by CAP engagements. CAP engagements consist of phased pre -deployment engagements designed to evaluate customer -specific use cases, demonstrate deployment feasibility, and integrate Digit into customer workflows prior to broader commercial deployment. Revenue is recognized over the period the services are performed using a measure of progress that reflects the transfer of the integrated service to the customer. CAP engagements frequently serve as the initial commercial relationship with a customer and are intended to facilitate broader commercial deployment through either direct robot sales or robot deployment arrangements. Repair and Maintenance Revenue from repair, maintenance, parts, and other support services is recognized as goods are delivered or services are performed. Revenue from stand -ready support arrangements, where applicable, is recognized over the related service period. The relative contribution of these revenue streams is expected to evolve over time as customer deployments increase and commercial adoption of our robotic systems expands. Cost of goods sold Cost of products Cost of products primarily consists of materials, labor, freight, manufacturing overhead, depreciation of manufacturing assets, and inventory reserves, including charges associated with obsolete robot models, incurred in the production and sale of Digit robots and related ancillary hardware. Cost of products is recorded when the control of products is transferred to the customer. Cost of services Cost of services consists primarily of personnel -related costs, including salaries, benefits and stock based compensation, materials, depreciation, and other direct costs associated with CAP engagements, robot deployment arrangements, and repair, maintenance, and other support services. Cost of services is recognized as the related services are performed. Selling, general and administrative expenses Selling expenses primarily consist of personnel -related costs, including salaries, commissions, benefits and stock -based compensation, for employees performing bid, proposal, marketing and sales functions as well as allocations of facility and consulting costs. General and administrative expenses primarily consist of personnel -related costs, including salaries, benefits and stock -based compensation, for executive leadership and employees in legal, finance, accounting, human resources, information technology and other administrative functions as well as allocated facility and consulting costs. Research and development expenses Research and development expenses primarily consist of personnel -related costs, including salaries, benefits and stock -based compensation, costs of materials, costs of consultants and allocated facility costs associated with the research, engineering, design and development of our next generation humanoid robots. 242 Table of Contents Interest income Interest income, net consists primarily of interest earned on interest -bearing cash deposits and short -term , highly liquid investments. Other, net Other income (expense) is composed primarily of credit card rebates and employee retention credits, offset by losses on the sale of property and equipment. Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates Our consolidated financial statements included in this proxy statement/prospectus have been prepared in accordance with GAAP. Preparation of the financial statements requires our management to make judgments, estimates and assumptions that impact the reported amounts of net sales and expenses, assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities. We consider an accounting judgment, estimate or assumption to be critical when the estimate or assumption is complex in nature or requires a high degree of judgment and the use of different judgments, estimates and assumptions could have a material impact on our consolidated financial statements. We periodically review estimates and adjusts those estimates when facts and circumstances dictate. To the extent that there are material differences between these estimates and actual results, its financial condition or results of operations will be affected. While our significant accounting policies are described in Note 2 to our audited financial statements included elsewhere in this proxy statement/prospectus, we believe the following critical accounting policies are most important to understanding and evaluating our reported financial results. Revenue Recognition We recognize revenue from sales of robotics equipment, robot deployment arrangements, CAP engagements, and repair, maintenance, and other support services. Certain customer arrangements, particularly CAP engagements and contracts with multiple performance obligations, require management to exercise judgment in determining the timing of revenue recognition and the allocation of transaction price to the related performance obligations. Management also exercises judgment in estimating variable consideration, including customer incentives and other contractual adjustments, and in assessing progress toward completion for revenue recognized over time. These estimates are based on the specific terms of each customer arrangement and management’s expectations regarding contract performance. Changes in these estimates could affect the timing and amount of revenue recognized in future periods. Inventory Inventories are stated at the lower of average cost or net realizable value and consist primarily of raw materials and work in process. Management exercises judgment in determining inventory valuation, including the allocation of manufacturing costs to inventory and the estimation of excess and obsolete inventory reserves. 246 Table of Contents The determination of excess and obsolete inventory requires management to evaluate expected future demand, product lifecycle assumptions, engineering compatibility of components across robot models, and the expected recoverability of inventory through future production and commercial deployment. Management also evaluates whether materials are associated with commercial production activities or research and development efforts, as materials determined to be used solely for research and development are expensed as incurred. Changes in these assumptions could materially affect inventory valuation and the amount of inventory -related expense recognized in future periods. Property and Equipment Property and equipment consists primarily of robots deployed under robot deployment arrangements, construction in progress, and manufacturing equipment. Management exercises judgment in determining when internally manufactured robots are transferred from inventory into property and equipment and when those robots are considered placed into service, at which time depreciation begins. Management also exercises judgment in estimating the useful lives of robots and evaluating those assets for impairment. These estimates require consideration of expected deployment periods, product lifecycle assumptions, technological obsolescence, and expected future economic benefit. Changes in these assumptions could result in changes to estimated useful lives or the recognition of impairment charges in future periods. Contingently Redeemable Preferred Stock As all series of our preferred stock are contingently redeemable upon the occurrence of events not solely within our control, the preferred stock is presented as mezzanine equity, separate from the stockholders’ deficit section of the consolidated balance sheet. The preferred stock is initially recorded at the fair value determined on the issuance date. Adjustments to the fair value of the preferred stock to the current market value are not made each period. Rather, we assess whether the contingently redeemable preferred stock has become redeemable or the probability that the preferred stock will become redeemable in determining whether to record subsequent measurement adjustments. The Company’s Series A, A -1 , A -2 , A -3 , A -4 , B, B, C -1 and C -2 Preferred Stock are not currently redeemable or probable of becoming redeemable in the future period. Refer to Note 8 to our audited consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this proxy statement/prospectus for additional information. Stock-Based Compensation The Company grants stock options under its Equity Incentive Plan, which are accounted for as liability -classified awards due to the Company’s contractual repurchase rights associated with exercised awards. Liability -classified awards are initially measured at fair value on the grant date and subsequently remeasured to fair value at each reporting date until settlement or until the repurchase right lapse and the awards are no longer require liability classification. Changes in fair value are recognized as stock -based compensation expense and allocated between cost of goods sold, selling, general, and administrative expenses, and research and development expenses in the statement of operations, based on the function of the employees to whom the expense relates. The determination of the fair value of liability -classified awards requires significant judgment. Because the Company’s common stock is not publicly traded, the fair value of the underlying common stock is determined based on periodic independent third -party valuations that consider recent equity transactions, the Company’s operating and financial performance, comparable companies, market conditions, and other relevant factors. The fair value of the awards is estimated using the Black -Scholes option -pricing model, which incorporates assumptions including the expected term, expected volatility, risk -free interest rate, and expected dividend yield. Changes in these assumptions or in the estimated fair value of the Company’s common stock could materially affect the amount of stock -based compensation expense recognized in future periods. The Company accounts for forfeitures as they occur. 247 Table of Contents Recently Issued or Adopted Accounting Standards A description of recently issued and adopted accounting pronouncements are described in Note 2 to our audited consolidated financial statements and unaudited consolidated interim financial statements included elsewhere in this proxy statement/prospectus. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk Interest Rate Risk We had cash and cash equivalents of $103 million as of December 31, 2025. We hold our cash and cash equivalents for working capital purposes. Our cash and cash equivalents are held in cash deposits and money market funds. Due to the short -term nature of these instruments, we believe that we do not have any material exposure to changes in the fair value of cash and cash equivalents and available -for-sale securities due to changes in interest rates. Increasing interest rates, however, would reduce the value of our available -for-sale securities and declining interest rates would reduce our future interest income. The effect of a hypothetical 10% change in interest rates would not have a material impact on our financial statements. Concentrations of Credit Risk We deposit cash with financial institutions, and, at times, such balances may exceed federally insured limits. We believe the financial institutions that hold our cash and cash equivalents are financially sound and, accordingly, minimal credit risk exists with respect to cash and cash equivalents. Emerging Growth Company Status Section 102(b)(1) of the JOBS Act exempts emerging growth companies from being required to comply with new or revised financial accounting standards until private companies are required to comply with the new or revised financial accounting standards. The JOBS Act provides that a company can choose not to take advantage of the extended transition period and comply with the requirements that apply to non -emerging growth companies, and any such election to not take advantage of the extended transition period is irrevocable. The Post -Closing Company intends to take advantage of the benefits of this extended transition period and, following the consummation of the business combination, will be an emerging growth company (for the period described in the immediately succeeding paragraph) and will take advantage of the benefits of the extended transition period emerging growth company status permits. During the extended transition period, it may be difficult or impossible to compare the Post -Closing Company’s financial results with the financial results of another public company that complies with public company effective dates for accounting standard updates because of the potential differences in accounting standards used: The Post -Closing Company will remain an emerging growth company under the JOBS Act until the earlier of: • The last day of the fiscal year in which its total annual gross revenues are $1.235 billion or more. • The last day of the fiscal year following the fifth anniversary of the CCXI IPO. • The date on which it has issued more than $1.0 billion in non -convertible debt during the previous three years. • The date on which it is deemed to be a large accelerated filer. 248 Table of Contents EXECUTIVE AND DIRECTOR COMPENSATION CCXI Executive Officer and Director Compensation CCXI is an “emerging growth company,” as defined in the JOBS Act, and the following is intended to comply with the reduced disclosure requirements applicable to emerging growth companies. Board Composition Effective upon the Closing, the Post -Closing Company Board will consist of seven, but may consist of up to nine, directors, a majority of whom will be required to qualify as an independent director under Nasdaq rules. The Post -Closing Company Board will serve staggered terms divided into three classes, Class I, Class II and Class III, with members of each class serving staggered three (3) -year terms. The term of the initial Class I members of the Post -Closing Company Board shall expire at the first annual meeting of the stockholders of SPAC following the Closing, the term of the initial Class II members of the Post -Closing Company Board shall expire at the second annual meeting of the stockholders of SPAC following the Closing and the term of the initial Class III member of the Post -Closing Company Board shall expire at the third annual meeting of the stockholders of SPAC following the Closing. When considering whether directors and director nominees have the experience, qualifications, attributes and skills, taken as a whole, to enable the Post -Closing Company Board to satisfy its oversight responsibilities effectively in light of its business and structure, the Post -Closing Company Board expects to focus primarily on each person’s background and experience as reflected in the information discussed in each of the directors’ individual biographies set forth above in order to provide an appropriate mix of experience and skills relevant to the size and nature of its business. Director Independence Under Nasdaq rules, a director is not independent unless the Board of Directors affirmatively determines that he or she does not have a direct or indirect material relationship with the Post -Closing Company or any of its subsidiaries. In addition, the director must not be precluded from qualifying as independent under the per se bars set forth by Nasdaq rules. The Post -Closing Company Board will undertake a review of its composition, the composition of its committees and the independence of its directors and consider whether any director has a material relationship with the Post -Closing Company that could compromise his or her ability to exercise independent judgment in carrying out his or her responsibilities. Based upon information requested from and provided by each director concerning his or her background, employment and affiliations, including family relationships, the Post -Closing Company Board is expected to determine that             of the Post -Closing Company’s directors, do not have a relationship that would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment in carrying out the responsibilities of a director and that each of these directors qualifies as “independent” as that term is defined under Nasdaq rules. In making these determinations, the Post -Closing Company Board will consider the relationships that each non -employee director has with the Post -Closing Company and all other facts and circumstances the Post -Closing Company Board deemed relevant in determining their independence, including the director’s beneficial ownership of the Post -Closing Company Common Stock. 257 Table of Contents Board Committees The Post -Closing Company Board will direct the management of its business and affairs, as provided by Delaware law, and will conduct its business through meetings of the board of directors and standing committees. Role of the Post-Closing Company Board in Risk Oversight/Risk Committee Upon the consummation of the business combination, one of the key functions of the Post -Closing Company Board will be informed oversight of the Post -Closing Company’s risk management process. The Post -Closing Company Board does not anticipate having a standing risk management committee but rather anticipates administering this oversight function directly through the Post -Closing Company Board as a whole, as well as through various standing committees of the Post -Closing Company Board that address risks inherent in their respective areas of oversight. For example, the Post -Closing Company Board audit committee will be responsible for overseeing the management of risks 260 Table of Contents associated with the Post -Closing Company’s financial reporting, operational, privacy and cybersecurity, competition, legal, regulatory, compliance and reputational matters; and the Post -Closing Company’s compensation committee will oversee the management of risks associated with our compensation policies and programs. Oversight of Cybersecurity Risks The Post -Closing Company will face a number of risks, including cybersecurity risks and those other risks described under the section entitled “Risk Factors” included in this proxy statement/prospectus. The audit committee will be responsible for overseeing the steps management has taken with respect to cybersecurity risk exposure. As part of this oversight, the audit committee will receive regular reports from management of the Post -Closing Company on cybersecurity risk exposure and the actions management has taken to limit, monitor or control such exposures at its regularly scheduled meetings. Management will work with third -party service providers to maintain appropriate controls. We believe this division of responsibilities is the most effective approach for addressing the Post -Closing Company’s cybersecurity risks and that the Post -Closing Company Board leadership structure supports this approach. Limitation on Liability and Indemnification of Directors and Officers The Proposed Charter, which will be effective upon consummation of the business combination, contains provisions that, to the fullest extent permitted by the DGCL, eliminate the personal liability of the Post -Closing Company’s directors and certain officers for monetary damages resulting from breaches of certain fiduciary duties as a director or officer. The Proposed Charter and the Post -Closing Company’s bylaws require the Post -Closing Company to indemnify and advance expenses to, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, its directors, officers and agents. The Post -Closing Company plans to maintain a directors’ and officers’ insurance policy pursuant to which the Post -Closing Company’s directors and officers are insured against liability for actions taken in their capacities as directors and officers. Finally, the Proposed Charter and the Post -Closing Company’s bylaws prohibit any retroactive changes to the rights or protections or increasing the liability of any director or officer in effect at the time of the alleged occurrence of any act or omission to act giving rise to liability or indemnification. In addition, the Post -Closing Company will enter into separate indemnification agreements with the Post -Closing Company’s directors, officers, and certain employees containing provisions which are in some respects broader than the specific indemnification provisions contained in the DGCL. These agreements, among other things, require the Post -Closing Company to indemnify its directors and officers for certain expenses, including attorneys’ fees, judgments, fines and settlement amounts incurred by a director or officer in any action or proceeding arising out of their services as one of the Post -Closing Company’s directors or officers or any other company or enterprise to which the person provides services at the Post -Closing Company’s request. We believe these provisions in the Proposed Charter and the Post -Closing Company’s bylaws are necessary to attract and retain qualified persons as directors and officers for the Post -Closing Company following the completion of the business combination. Corporate Governance Guidelines and Code of Business Conduct The Post -Closing Company Board will adopt Corporate Governance Guidelines that address items such as the qualifications and responsibilities of its directors and director candidates and corporate governance policies and standards applicable to the Post -Closing Company. In addition, the Post -Closing Company Board will adopt a Code of Business Conduct and Ethics that applies to all of its employees, officers and directors, including its Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer and other executive and senior financial officers. The full text of the Post -Closing Company’s Corporate Governance Guidelines and its Code of Business Conduct and Ethics will be posted on the Corporate Governance portion of the Post -Closing Company’s website at www.agilityrobotics.com. Introduction On June 24, 2026, CCXI entered into the Merger Agreement with Merger Sub and Agility. CCXI is a blank check company formed in order to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June 4, 2025. On December 18, 2025, CCXI consummated its initial public offering of 41,400,000 CCXI public units, including 5,400,000 CCXI public units pursuant to the underwriters’ full exercise of the over -allotment option. The CCXI public units were sold at an offering price of $10.00 per unit, generating gross proceeds to CCXI of $414,000,000. Simultaneously with the consummation of the CCXI IPO and the exercise of the underwriters’ over -allotment option, CCXI consummated the private placement of 500,000 CCXI private placement units to the Sponsor at a price of $10.00 per unit, generating total proceeds of $5,000,000. Transaction costs amounted to $19,618,232, consisting of $3,000,000 of underwriting fees, $15,990,000 of deferred underwriting fees (of which $1,500,000 has been paid and $14,490,000 remains deferred) and $628,232 of other offering costs. Agility Robotics, Inc. was organized in 2015 under the laws of the State of Delaware as a spinoff of Oregon State University, to commercialize research from the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory on bipedal locomotion. Since inception, Agility has developed several versions of a bipedal robot, referred to as Digit. Historically, Digit has been sold as a unit, deployed under robot deployment arrangements, and used for short -term customer acceleration program engagements (historically referred to as proof -of-concept or POC), with strategic partners and prospective long -term customers. These efforts are still largely considered to be research and development, and Agility is currently considered to be a development stage company. Agility is headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously in Tangent, Oregon, with offices located in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and San Jose, California. CCXI is providing the following unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information to aid in the analysis of the financial aspects of the business combination and other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement. The following unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information presents the combination of the financial information of CCXI and Agility, adjusted to give effect to the business combination and other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement. The following unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information has been prepared in accordance with Article 11 of Regulation S -X . The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial statements give effect to the business combination and other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement as described in this proxy statement/prospectus. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined balance sheet as of June 30, 2026 combines the historical unaudited condensed balance sheet of Agility with the historical unaudited condensed balance sheet of CCXI on a pro forma basis as if the business combination and the other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement, summarized below, had been consummated on June 30, 2026. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined statement of operations for the six months ended June 30, 2026 combines the historical unaudited condensed statement of operations of Agility for the six months ended June 30, 2026 and the historical unaudited condensed statement of operations of CCXI for the six months ended June 30, 2026. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined statement of operations for the year ended December 31, 2025, combines the historical audited statement of operations of Agility for the year ended December 31, 2025, with the historical audited statement of operations of CCXI for the period from June 4, 2025 (inception) through December 31, 2025. Although CCXI was incorporated as a Cayman Islands exempted company on June 4, 2025, for purposes of unaudited pro forma condensed combined statements of operation for the six months ended June 30, 2026 and the year ended December 31, 2025, the business combination and other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement have been given effect as if they had been consummated as of January 1, 2025. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial statements have been prepared for informational purposes only and are not necessarily indicative of what the Post -Closing Company’s condensed financial position or results of operations actually would have been had the business combination been consummated on the dates indicated above, nor are they necessarily indicative of future results of operations. In addition, the unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial statements do not purport to project the future financial position or operating results of the Post -Closing Company. 262 Table of Contents The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information was derived from and should be read in conjunction with the following historical financial statements and the accompanying notes, which are included elsewhere in this proxy statement/prospectus: • audited historical financial statements of CCXI for the period from June 4, 2025 (inception) through December 31, 2025; • unaudited historical condensed financial statements of CCXI as of and for the six months ended June 30, 2026; • audited historical financial statements of Agility for the year ended December 31, 2025; • unaudited historical condensed financial statements of Agility as of and for the six months ended June 30, 2026; and • other information relating to CCXI and Agility included in this proxy statement/prospectus, including the Merger Agreement and the description of certain terms thereof and the financial and operational condition of CCXI and Agility. Description of the Business Combination Pursuant to the Merger Agreement and the related agreements, and upon the terms and subject to the conditions set forth therein, CCXI will acquire Agility and Agility will become a publicly traded company through the business combination. The business combination consists of (a) the transfer of the registration of CCXI by way of continuation from the Cayman Islands to the State of Delaware (the “ Domestication ”), and (b) following the Domestication, the merger of Merger Sub with and into Agility, with Agility as the surviving entity and as a wholly -owned subsidiary of CCXI. Subject to the terms and conditions of the Merger Agreement, the value of the aggregate consideration to be paid to Agility stockholders, holders of Agility options and Agility convertible securities will be $2,500,000,000. At the Effective Time, each share of Agility common stock issued and outstanding immediately prior to the Effective Time (other than Excluded Shares and Dissenting Shares) will be automatically cancelled and converted into the right to receive a number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock equal to the Exchange Ratio. The Exchange Ratio is based on the per share Equity Value (calculated in accordance with the Merger Agreement). Subject to the assumptions described herein, as of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, shares of Post -Closing Company common stock will be issued for each issued and outstanding share of Agility common stock (after giving effect to the Conversions). Following the business combination and related events and based on the estimated Exchange Ratio of , the following will be outstanding (excluding issuance of shares related to the PIPE Subscription Agreements): • an estimated 201,894,151 shares of Post -Closing Company common stock issued to Agility’s stockholders; • Post -Closing Company options related to the assumption of Agility stock options, which will be exercisable for an estimated 54,435,468 shares of Post -Closing Company common stock; • 500,000 shares of Post -Closing Company common stock in exchange for CCXI private placement shares held by the Sponsor subject to certain provisions under the Sponsor Agreement; • 13,800,000 shares of Post -Closing Company common stock in exchange for CCXI Founder Shares held by the Sponsor subject to certain provisions under the Sponsor Agreement; • 41,400,000 CCXI public shares or 0 shares, under the No Redemption Scenario or Maximum Redemptions Scenario, respectively, of the Post -Closing Company common stock held by CCXI public shareholders. The business combination will occur based on the following transactions as contemplated by the Merger Agreement: • the Domestication and related automatic conversion of each CCXI Class A Ordinary Share issued and outstanding immediately prior to the Domestication into one share of CCXI common stock; • the Merger of Merger Sub with and into Agility, with Agility continuing as the surviving entity and as a wholly owned subsidiary of CCXI; 263 Table of Contents • each share of Agility common stock, including shares of Agility common stock issued upon the pre -Closing conversions of Agility preferred stock, Agility SAFEs and all equity securities issued or issuable in connection with a Permitted Bridge Financing (to the extent not already constituting Agility SAFEs), will be automatically surrendered and shall cease to exist, and will be exchanged for the right to receive, in the aggregate, the Merger Consideration; and • the assumption of each outstanding and unexercised Agility option (whether or not vested) will be assumed by the Post -Closing Company and become an option to purchase shares of Post -Closing Company common stock, on the same terms and conditions (including applicable vesting, exercise and expiration provisions) as applied to each such Agility option immediately prior to the Effective Time (each an “ Exchanged Option ”), except that (1) the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock subject to such Exchanged Option will equal (a) the number of shares of Agility common stock that were subject to such option immediately prior to the Effective Time multiplied by (b) the Exchange Ratio, rounded down to the nearest whole share, and (2) the per share exercise price will equal the quotient of (a) the exercise price per share of Agility common stock at which such option was exercisable immediately prior to the Effective Time, divided by (b) the Exchange Ratio, rounded up to the nearest whole cent. Available Closing SPAC Cash shall not be less than $200.0 million, which is calculated as follows: • all amounts in the trust account (after reduction for the aggregate amount of payments required to be made in connection with any valid CCXI public shareholder redemptions of CCXI public shares and any permitted withdrawals (as defined in the CCXI current articles of association), but before payment of any CCXI or Agility transaction expenses and repayment of any Sponsor loans, if any), plus • the net proceeds of any incremental financing raised by CCXI or Agility in connection with the Transactions, including the PIPE Investment in accordance with the terms and conditions of the PIPE Subscription Agreements. Other agreements that are entered into in connection with the business combination are summarized below: • Subscription Agreements — In connection with the execution of the Merger Agreement, CCXI entered into the PIPE Subscription Agreements with PIPE Investors. Pursuant to the terms of the PIPE Subscription Agreements, CCXI has agreed to issue and sell to the PIPE Investors and the PIPE Investors have agreed to buy, 20,102,500 shares of CCXI common stock at a purchase price of $10.00 per share for an aggregate commitment of $201,025,000. • Agility SAFEs — In July 2026, Agility authorized up to $100 million of additional financing through the issuance and sale of simple agreements for future equity, which Agility expects to convert into approximately 1,348,000 shares of Agility common stock. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, Agility has raised $100 million through the issuance and sale of such Agility SAFEs. Under this method of accounting, CCXI, which is the legal acquirer, will be treated as the accounting acquiree for financial reporting purposes and Agility, which is the legal acquiree, will be treated as the accounting acquirer for financial reporting purposes. Accordingly, the consolidated assets, liabilities and results of operations of Agility will become the historical financial statements of the Post -Closing Company, and CCXI’s assets, liabilities and results of operations will be consolidated with Agility’s beginning on the acquisition date. For accounting purposes, the financial statements of the Post -Closing Company will represent a continuation of the financial statements of Agility with the business combination being treated as the equivalent of Agility issuing stock for the net assets of CCXI, accompanied by a recapitalization. The net assets of CCXI will be stated at historical costs, which are expected to approximate fair value, and no goodwill or other intangible assets will be recorded. Operations prior to the business combination will be presented as those of Agility in future reports of the Post -Closing Company. Agility was determined to be the accounting acquirer under both the redemption scenarios presented based on evaluation of the following facts and circumstances: • Agility stockholders comprise a relative majority of greater than 72.7% of the voting power of the Post -Closing Company under both the redemption scenarios; • Agility will have the ability to nominate a majority of the members of the board of directors of the Post -Closing Company; • Agility’s operations prior to the business combination comprise the only ongoing operations of Post -Closing Company; • Agility’s senior management will comprise the senior management of the Post -Closing Company; • The ongoing operations of Agility will become the operations of the Post -Closing Company; and • Agility’s headquarters will become the Post -Closing Company’s headquarters. The final allocation of consideration payable to Agility equity holders will be determined upon the completion of the business combination and related events and could differ materially from the two scenarios presented. Loss per Share Represents the net loss per share calculated using the historical weighted -average shares outstanding and the issuance of additional shares in connection with the business combination and related transactions, assuming the shares were outstanding since January 1, 2025. In the case of shares presented as being held by Agility stockholders, the tables below assumes that Agility preferred stock outstanding as of December 31, 2025 had converted to Agility common stock and that each such share of Agility common stock was exchanged for a number of shares equal to the assumed Exchange Ratio as of January 1, 2025. In the case of stock options presented in the table below showing potentially dilutive instruments, the table assumes that such stock options were exchanged applying the assumed Exchange Ratio as of January 1, 2025. Net income loss per share was computed using the two -class method required for participating securities. The two -class method requires income available to ordinary shareholders for the period to be allocated between ordinary shares and participating securities based upon their respective rights to receive dividends as if all income for the period had been distributed. Net losses are not allocated to these participating securities as there are no contractual obligations that require participation in the Post -Closing Company’s losses. As the business combination is being reflected as if it had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period presented, the calculation of weighted -average shares outstanding for basic and diluted net loss per share assumes that the shares issuable relating to the business combination and related transactions have been outstanding for the entire periods presented. When assuming the Maximum Redemptions Scenario, this calculation is adjusted to eliminate such shares for the entire period. Basic and diluted earnings per share are the same for each class of common stock because they are entitled to the same liquidation and dividend rights.
